translation: And so it was that the Great Sage had reached the banks of the River Flood, transformed himself into the form of Second Son of the Fairy, and descended from the clouds straight into the temple. The demon wardens could not recognize him, each of them bowing in greeting. He took his seat in the middle, tallying the offerings: Li Hu’s sacrifice of livestock, Zhang Long’s wish for protection, Zhao Jia’s petition for a son, and Qian Bing’s plea for recovery from illness. Just as he was inspecting them, someone reported, "Another grandmaster has arrived." The demon wardens hurriedly looked on, all stunned. The True Monarch asked, "Is there any such thing as a Great Sage who came here just now?" The demon wardens replied, "We did not see any Great Sage; only one grandmaster was here tallying the offerings." The True Monarch barged in, but the Monkey King, upon seeing him, revealed his true form and said, "Son, no need to shout; the temple is already owned by the Sun family." This True Monarch then raised his trident and struck at the face. The Monkey King evaded the blow, drew his tiny needle, and with a flick, made it the size of a bowl, and charged forward to engage in combat. The two bickered and fought, leaving the temple, moving through half-misty, half-cloudy air, continuing to battle as they went. They returned to Flower and Fruit Mountain, which caused the Four Heavenly Kings and others to tighten their guard. Liu and Zhang the Grand Wardens, meeting the True Monarch, surrounded the Monkey King, each determined to defeat him.
source_text: 却说那大圣已至灌江口，摇身一变，变作二郎爷爷的模样，按下云头，径入庙里。鬼判不能相认，一个个磕头迎接。他坐中间，点查香火：见李虎拜还的三牲，张龙许下的保福，赵甲求子的文书，钱丙告病的良愿。正看处，有人报：“又一个爷爷来了。”众鬼判急急观看，无不惊心。真君却道：“有个甚么齐天大圣，才来这里否？”众鬼判道：“不曾见甚么大圣，只有一个爷爷在里面查点哩。”真君撞进门，大圣见了，现出本相道：“郎君不消嚷，庙宇已姓孙了。”这真君即举三尖两刃神锋，劈脸就砍。那猴王使个身法，让过神锋，掣出那绣花针儿，幌一幌，碗来粗细，赶到前，对面相还。两个嚷嚷闹闹，打出庙门，半雾半云，且行且战，复打到花果山，慌得那四大天王等众，提防愈紧。这康、张太尉等迎着真君，合力努力，把那美猴王围绕不题。
gt_translation: However, he said that the great sage had reached the mouth of Guanjiang, changed his body, changed into the appearance of Erlang's grandfather, pressed the cloud head, and entered the temple. The ghosts couldn't recognize each other, and they kowtowed to them one by one. He sat in the middle and counted the incense: seeing the three sacrifices that Li Hubai paid back, the blessing promised by Zhang Long, the document that Zhao Jia asked for a son, and the good wishes of Qian Bing to report illness. Just looking at the place, someone reported: "Another grandfather is here." The ghosts watched anxiously, and they were all startled. However, the true monarch said, "Is there a great sage Equaling the Sky that came here?" The ghosts said, "I have never seen any great sage, but only a grandfather checked it out." The true monarch slammed into the door. Now, he showed his true nature: "Lang-jun doesn't need to shout, the temple's surname is Sun." This real monarch raised three sharp and two-edged divine sharp edges, and chopped his face. The Monkey King made a move, passed Shen Feng, took out the embroidery needle, made a look, the thickness of the bowl, rushed to the front, and returned it to the opposite side. The two made a fuss and fought outside the temple gate. It was half fog and half cloud. This Kang, Taiwei Zhang and others faced the real monarch and worked together to surround the beautiful monkey king.

human_translations.translator_1: With a shake of his body, he changed into the form of Holy Father Erlang. Lowering the direction of his cloud, he went straight into the temple, and the demon magistrates could not tell that he was not the real Erlang. Every one of them, in fact, kowtowed to receive him. He sat down in the middle and began to examine the various offerings; the three kinds of sacrificial meat brought by Li Hu, the votive offering of Zhang Long, the petition for a son by Zhao Jia, and the request for healing by Qian Bing. As he was looking at these, someone made the report, “Another Holy Father has arrived!” The various demon magistrates went quickly to look and were terror-stricken, one and all. The Immortal Master asked, “Did a so-called Great Sage, Equal to Heaven, come here?” “We haven’t seen any Great Sage,” said the demon magistrates. “But another Holy Father is in there examining the offerings.” The Immortal Master crashed through the door; seeing him, the Great Sage revealed his true form and said, “There’s no need for the little boy to strive anymore! Sun is now the name of this temple!” The Immortal Master lifted his divine lance of three points and two blades and struck, but the Monkey King with agile body was quick to move out of the way. He whipped out that embroidery needle of his, and with one wave caused it to take on the thickness of a rice bowl. Rushing forward, he engaged Erlang face to face. Starting at the door of the temple, the two combatants fought all the way back to the Flower-Fruit Mountain, treading on clouds and mists and shouting insults at each other. The Four Devarājas and their followers were so startled by their appearance that they stood guard with even greater vigilance, while the grand marshals joined the Immortal Master to surround the Handsome Monkey King.
human_translations.translator_2: But after the Great Sage had got there, he changed himself into the form of the Divine Kinsman himself, came down from the clouds and entered a temple. As no one could distinguish the fraud, all came and kowtowed, and he in their midst surveyed the burning of incense, and then read the written prayers and heard Li Hu paying his vows of three animals for sacrifice, Zhang Long offering thanksgiving for blessings received, Zhao Jia begging for a son, and Jian Bing begging to be relieved of his duties on account of ill health. As this performance was going on, there came a man to announce that an old man had come. All quickly turned round to see and were greatly frightened at his demeanor. The Divine Kinsman, for he was the old man, said, “Has the Great Sage, the Equal of Heaven come here?” They replied, “No, we have not seen the Great Sage, but there is an old man inside burning incense.” The Divine Kinsman rushed inside. The Great Sage at sight of him appeared in his true form and said, “Do not make any disturbance, Prince, the temple belongs to the Sun family.” The Divine Kinsman raised his trident, with its double edged blades, rushed on him to cut him down, but the Monkey King evaded his thrust, took out his embroidery needle from his ear and when it grew as large in circumference as an arm or a leg, rushed to meet him and there was a fierce struggle between them. They got out of the temple and fought in the air as they went, until they reached the Mountain Garden, where they terrified the Four Great Guardians of Heaven and their followers, who were surrounding the place. The Four Governors and the Two Commanders-in-chief came to meet the Divine Kinsman and with all their might tried to surround the Great Sage. Then the Chief, having called the six brethren and their soldiers together to take the Monkey King, returned to Heaven to report.
human_translations.translator_3: As soon as he reached the Guan, Monkey changed himself into an exact likeness of Erlang, received the obeisances of Erlang’s subordinates, and set to officiating in his nemesis’s own temple. Not long after, however, the real Erlang arrived, and his officials rushed out to see the doppelgänger. “Has a so-named Great Sage Equal to Heaven been here?” Erlang wanted to know. “No, no one of that name. But there is another version of you inside.” After the real Erlang charged at his impersonator, Monkey took his true form. “Welcome to the Temple of Monkey!” Erlang struck at Monkey’s face with his tri-pointed lance, but Monkey dodged, and the two of them jousted their way back to Flower-Fruit Mountain. Back in Heaven, the Jade Emperor and his court were wondering why they had heard no news of Monkey for some while.
human_translations.translator_4: The Great Sage had already arrived there, changed himself into the likeness of the god Erlang with a shake of his body, put away his cloud, and gone into the temple. The demon judges did not realize who he really was, so they all kowtowed to welcome him. He took his seat in the middle of the temple, and inspected the offerings: the beef, mutton and pork presented by one Li Hu, the ex-voto promised by a Zhang Long, the letter from a Zhao Jia asking for a son, and one Qian Bing's prayer for recovery from illness. As he was looking round it was announced that another Lord Erlang had arrived. All the demon judges hurried to look, and they were all astonished. The True Lord Erlang asked, “Has a so-called Great Sage Equaling Heaven been here?” “We haven't seen any Great Sages,” they replied, “only another god who's looking around inside.” The True Lord rushed in through the gates, and as soon as the Great Sage saw him he reverted to his own appearance and said, “There's no point in shouting, sir. This temple's mine now.” The True Lord raised his double-bladed trident and swung at the Monkey King's head, but the Monkey King dodged the blow by magic, took his embroidery needle, shook it till it was as thick as a bowl, and rushed forward to meet the attack. Shouting and yelling, they fought their way out through the gates, and went on fighting through the mists and clouds all the way back to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit. The Four Heavenly Kings and all their soldiers were so alarmed that they kept an even tighter guard. Marshals Kang and Zhang and the others came to meet the True Lord, and combined their efforts to surround the Handsome Monkey King. But of this no more for now.

translation: Meanwhile, the Great Sage had arrived at the Riverbank Fort. He changed himself into the form of Little Dragon King and alighted from the clouds, entering the temple. The ghost attendants were unable to recognize him, each of them bowing to greet him. He sat in the middle and examined the offerings: Li Hu’s offering of sacrificial animals, Zhang Long’s promise of blessings, Zhao Jia’s petition for a child, and Qian Bing’s vow for recovery. Just as he was reviewing the offerings, someone reported, “Another grandmaster has arrived.” The ghost attendants rushed to look, each feeling their hearts racing. The True Emperor said, “Is there such a thing as the Great Sage Equal to Heaven who has just arrived here?” The ghost attendants said, “We did not see the Great Sage; there is only one grandmaster inside checking the offerings.” The True Emperor burst into the temple. The Great Sage saw him and revealed his true form, saying, “Young Master need not shout; the temple is now owned by the Sun Family.” The True Emperor then raised his three-cornered, two-edged divine saber and chopped at him. The Great Sage used a technique to dodge the saber and drew his embroidery-thread needle, which he waved until it was as thick as a bowl, charging forward to meet the True Emperor in battle. They brawled and quarreled, leaving the temple, and a half-misty half-cloudy trail followed them. They returned to Flower and Fruit Mountain, causing the Four Heavenly Kings and the rest to be even more alert. The Counts Kang and Zhang, along with the other grandmasters, surrounded the True Emperor and fought with him, not pausing to describe it.

translation: And so, the Great Sage had arrived at the Ganshui River Pass and transformed himself into the form of Young Master Láng. He pressed down his cloud and entered the temple. The two made a fuss and fought outside the temple gate. It was half fog and half cloud. human_translations.translator_1: With a shake of his body, he changed into the form of Holy Father Erlang. Lowering the direction of his cloud, he went straight into the temple, and the demon magistrates could not tell that he was not the real Erlang. Every one of them, in fact, kowtowed to receive him. He sat down in the middle and began to examine the various offerings; the three kinds of sacrificial meat brought by Li Hu, the votive offering of Zhang Long, the petition for a son by Zhao Jia, and the request for healing by Qian Bing. As he was looking at these, someone made the report, “Another Holy Father has arrived!” The various demon magistrates went quickly to look and were terror-stricken, one and all. The Immortal Master asked, “Did a so-called Great Sage, Equal to Heaven, come here?” “We haven’t seen any Great Sage,” said the demon magistrates. “But another Holy Father is in there examining the offerings.” The Immortal Master crashed through the door; seeing him, the Great Sage revealed his true form and said, “There’s no need for the little boy to strive anymore! Sun is now the name of this temple!” The Immortal Master lifted his divine lance of three points and two blades and struck, but the Monkey King with agile body was quick to move out of the way. He whipped out that embroidery needle of his, and with one wave caused it to take on the thickness of a rice bowl. Rushing forward, he engaged Erlang face to face. Starting at the door of the temple, the two combatants fought all the way back to the Flower-Fruit Mountain, treading on clouds and mists and shouting insults at each other. The Four Devarājas and their followers were so startled by their appearance that they stood guard with even greater vigilance, while the grand marshals joined the Immortal Master to surround the Handsome Monkey King.
human_translations.translator_2: But after the Great Sage had got there, he changed himself into the form of the Divine Kinsman himself, came down from the clouds and entered a temple. As no one could distinguish the fraud, all came and kowtowed, and he in their midst surveyed the burning of incense, and then read the written prayers and heard Li Hu paying his vows of three animals for sacrifice, Zhang Long offering thanksgiving for blessings received, Zhao Jia begging for a son, and Jian Bing begging to be relieved of his duties on account of ill health. As this performance was going on, there came a man to announce that an old man had come. All quickly turned round to see and were greatly frightened at his demeanor. The Divine Kinsman, for he was the old man, said, “Has the Great Sage, the Equal of Heaven come here?” They replied, “No, we have not seen the Great Sage, but there is an old man inside burning incense.” The Divine Kinsman rushed inside. The Great Sage at sight of him appeared in his true form and said, “Do not make any disturbance, Prince, the temple belongs to the Sun family.” The Divine Kinsman raised his trident, with its double edged blades, rushed on him to cut him down, but the Monkey King evaded his thrust, took out his embroidery needle from his ear and when it grew as large in circumference as an arm or a leg, rushed to meet him and there was a fierce struggle between them. They got out of the temple and fought in the air as they went, until they reached the Mountain Garden, where they terrified the Four Great Guardians of Heaven and their followers, who were surrounding the place. The Four Governors and the Two Commanders-in-chief came to meet the Divine Kinsman and with all their might tried to surround the Great Sage. Then the Chief, having called the six brethren and their soldiers together to take the Monkey King, returned to Heaven to report.
human_translations.translator_3: As soon as he reached the Guan, Monkey changed himself into an exact likeness of Erlang, received the obeisances of Erlang’s subordinates, and set to officiating in his nemesis’s own temple. Not long after, however, the real Erlang arrived, and his officials rushed out to see the doppelgänger. “Has a so-named Great Sage Equal to Heaven been here?” Erlang wanted to know. “No, no one of that name. But there is another version of you inside.” After the real Erlang charged at his impersonator, Monkey took his true form. “Welcome to the Temple of Monkey!” Erlang struck at Monkey’s face with his tri-pointed lance, but Monkey dodged, and the two of them jousted their way back to Flower-Fruit Mountain. Back in Heaven, the Jade Emperor and his court were wondering why they had heard no news of Monkey for some while.
human_translations.translator_4: The Great Sage had already arrived there, changed himself into the likeness of the god Erlang with a shake of his body, put away his cloud, and gone into the temple. The demon judges did not realize who he really was, so they all kowtowed to welcome him. He took his seat in the middle of the temple, and inspected the offerings: the beef, mutton and pork presented by one Li Hu, the ex-voto promised by a Zhang Long, the letter from a Zhao Jia asking for a son, and one Qian Bing's prayer for recovery from illness. As he was looking round it was announced that another Lord Erlang had arrived. All the demon judges hurried to look, and they were all astonished. The True Lord Erlang asked, “Has a so-called Great Sage Equaling Heaven been here?” “We haven't seen any Great Sages,” they replied, “only another god who's looking around inside.” The True Lord rushed in through the gates, and as soon as the Great Sage saw him he reverted to his own appearance and said, “There's no point in shouting, sir. This temple's mine now.” The True Lord raised his double-bladed trident and swung at the Monkey King's head, but the Monkey King dodged the blow by magic, took his embroidery needle, shook it till it was as thick as a bowl, and rushed forward to meet the attack. Shouting and yelling, they fought their way out through the gates, and went on fighting through the mists and clouds all the way back to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit. The Four Heavenly Kings and all their soldiers were so alarmed that they kept an even tighter guard. translation: After thus dispelling her misgivings about him, he found the quiet tête-à-tête by the window too long; he tapped the lectern with his knuckles and then with his fist. The student glanced briefly over the woman’s shoulder at K, but was not disturbed, and even pressed closer to her and clasped her. She lowered her head deeply, as if listening attentively; he kissed her as she bent down, loudly on the neck, without interrupting his speech much. K saw in this the confirmation of the student’s tyranny, as described by the woman, and stood up, pacing back and forth in the room. He thought about how to get rid of the student as quickly as possible, and was not displeased when the student, apparently annoyed by K’s walking around, which had become almost a trampling, remarked: “If you are impatient, you can leave. You could have left earlier, no one would have missed you. Yes, you should have left immediately, and quickly.” This remark might have expressed all kinds of anger, but it also contained the arrogance of a future court official speaking to an unpleasant defendant. K stood very close to him and said smilingly, “I am indeed impatient, that is true, but this impatience can be most easily overcome by your leaving. If, however, perhaps you came here to study – I heard that you are a student – I will be glad to make way for you and leave with the woman. You will have to study much more before you become a judge, however. I know your court system only slightly, but I assume that it is not enough to do it merely with rough talk, which you know to deliver quite unseemly well.” “He shouldn’t have been allowed to walk around so freely,” the student said, as if explaining K’s offensive words to the woman, “it was a mistake. I told the examining judge. He should at least have been confined to a room during the questioning. The examining judge can be incomprehensible at times.” “Empty words,” said K and stretched out his hand to the woman, “come.” “Oh, so that’s it,” said the student, “no, no, you won’t get them.” And with a strength he did not seem to possess, he lifted her onto one arm and ran with bent back, looking lovingly up at her, toward the door. A certain fear of K could be recognized here, but despite that, the student still dared to provoke K by caressing and pressing the woman’s arm with his free hand. K ran a few steps beside him, ready to grab him and strangle him if necessary, until the woman said: “It’s no use, the examining judge has me, I cannot go with you, this little brat,” she ran her hand over the student’s face, “this little brat won’t let me.” “And you don’t want to be set free!” K shouted and placed his hand on the student’s shoulder, who snarled at him with his teeth. “No!” the woman cried and pushed K away with both hands, “no, no, not that, what are you thinking of! That would be my ruin. Let him go, please, let him go. He’s only carrying me to him as he’s ordered.” “Then let him run, and I’ll never see you again,” K said angrily, pushed the student in the back, and he stumbled briefly, only to spring higher with his burden in sheer joy at not having fallen. K walked after them slowly, realizing that this was the first clear defeat he had suffered from these people. Of course, there was no reason to be scared about that; he only received this defeat because he sought out the fight. If he stayed at home and led his usual life, he would be ten times superior to every one of these people and could easily sweep each one aside with a kick. He imagined the most absurd scene, for instance, if this pitiful student, this puffed-up child, this hunchbacked bearded man, would kneel before Elsa’s bed and beg for mercy with his hands folded. K liked this image so much that he decided that if the opportunity ever arose, he would take the student along to Elsa.
source_text: Nachdem er auf diese Weise die Bedenken gegen die Frau beseitigt hatte, wurde ihm das leise Zwiegespräch am Fenster zu lang, er klopfte mit den Knöcheln auf das Podium und dann auch mit der Faust. Der Student sah kurz über die Schulter der Frau hinweg nach K. hin, ließ sich aber nicht stören, ja drückte sich sogar eng an die Frau und umfaßte sie. Sie senkte tief den Kopf, als höre sie ihm aufmerksam zu, er küßte sie, als sie sich bückte, laut auf den Hals, ohne sich im Reden wesentlich zu unterbrechen. K. sah darin die Tyrannei bestätigt, die der Student nach den klagen der Frau über sie ausübte, stand auf und ging im Zimmer auf und ab. Er überlegte unter Seitenblicken nach dem Studenten, wie er ihn möglichst schnell wegschaffen könnte, und es war ihm daher nicht unwillkommen, als der Student, offenbar gestört durch K.s Herumgehen, das schon zeitweilig zu einem Trampeln ausgeartet war, bemerkte: »Wenn Sie ungeduldig sind, können Sie weggehen. Sie hätten auch schon früher weggehen können, es hätte Sie niemand vermißt. Ja, Sie hätten sogar weggehen sollen, und zwar schon bei meinem Eintritt, und zwar schleunigst.« Es mochte in dieser Bemerkung alle mögliche Wut zum Ausdruck kommen, jedenfalls lag darin aber auch der Hochmut des künftigen Gerichtsbeamten, der zu einem mißliebigen Angeklagten sprach. K. blieb ganz nahe bei ihm stehen und sagte lächelnd: »Ich bin ungeduldig, das ist richtig, aber diese Ungeduld wird am leichtesten dadurch zu beseitigen sein, daß Sie uns verlassen. Wenn Sie aber vielleicht hergekommen sind, um zu studieren – ich hörte, daß Sie Student sind –, so will ich Ihnen gerne Platz machen und mit der Frau weggehen. Sie werden übrigens noch viel studieren müssen, ehe Sie Richter werden. Ich kenne zwar Ihr Gerichtswesen noch nicht sehr genau, nehme aber an, daß es mit groben Reden allein, die Sie allerdings schon unverschämt gut zu führen wissen, noch lange nicht getan ist.« »Man hätte ihn nicht so frei herumlaufen lassen sollen«, sagte der Student, als wolle er der Frau eine Erklärung für K.s beleidigende Rede geben, »es war ein Mißgriff. Ich habe es dem Untersuchungsrichter gesagt. Man hätte ihn zwischen den Verhören zumindest in seinem Zimmer halten sollen. Der Untersuchungsrichter ist manchmal unbegreiflich.« »Unnütze Reden«, sagte K. und streckte die Hand nach der Frau aus, »kommen Sie.« »Ach so«, sagte der Student, »nein, nein, die bekommen Sie nicht«, und mit einer Kraft, die man ihm nicht zugetraut hätte, hob er sie auf einen Arm und lief mit gebeugtem Rücken, zärtlich zu ihr aufsehend, zur Tür. Eine gewisse Angst vor K. war hierbei nicht zu verkennen, trotzdem wagte er es, K. noch zu reizen, indem er mit der freien Hand den Arm der Frau streichelte und drückte. K. lief ein paar Schritte neben ihm her, bereit, ihn zu fassen und, wenn es sein mußte, zu würgen, da sagte die Frau: »Es hilft nichts, der Untersuchungsrichter läßt mich holen, ich darf nicht mit Ihnen gehen, dieses kleine Scheusal«, sie fuhr hierbei dem Studenten mit der Hand übers Gesicht, »dieses kleine Scheusal läßt mich nicht.« »Und Sie wollen nicht befreit werden!« schrie K. und legte die Hand auf die Schulter des Studenten, der mit den Zähnen nach ihr schnappte. »Nein!« rief die Frau und wehrte K. mit beiden Händen ab, »nein, nein, nur das nicht, woran denken Sie denn! Das wäre mein Verderben. Lassen Sie ihn doch, o bitte, lassen Sie ihn doch. Er führt ja nur den Befehl des Untersuchungsrichters aus und trägt mich zu ihm.« »Dann mag er laufen und Sie will ich nie mehr sehen«, sagte K. wütend vor Enttäuschung und gab dem Studenten einen Stoß in den Rücken, daß er kurz stolperte, um gleich darauf, vor Vergnügen darüber, daß er nicht gefallen war, mit seiner Last desto höher zu springen. K. ging ihnen langsam nach, er sah ein, daß das die erste zweifellose Niederlage war, die er von diesen Leuten erfahren hatte. Es war natürlich kein Grund, sich deshalb zu ängstigen, er erhielt die Niederlage nur deshalb, weil er den Kampf aufsuchte. Wenn er zu Hause bliebe und sein gewohntes Leben führte, war er jedem dieser Leute tausendfach überlegen und konnte jeden mit einem Fußtritt von seinem Wege räumen. Und er stellte sich die allerlächerlichste Szene vor, die es zum Beispiel geben würde, wenn dieser klägliche Student, dieses aufgeblasene Kind, dieser krumme Bartträger vor Elsas Bett knien und mit gefalteten Händen um Gnade bitten würde. K. gefiel diese Vorstellung so, daß er beschloß, wenn sich nur irgendeine Gelegenheit dafür ergeben sollte, den Studenten einmal zu Elsa mitzunehmen.

Glancing sideways toward the student, he contemplated the quickest way to get rid of him, and so he was happy enough when the student, apparently disturbed by K.’s pacing, which had meanwhile degenerated into full-blown tromping, remarked: “If you’re impatient, why don’t you leave? translation: After thus dispelling the woman's reservations about him, he found the whispered conversation by the window too tedious, and rapped on the podium with his knuckles, and then with his fist. The student briefly glanced over the woman's shoulder at K, but was not disturbed, and even pressed himself closer to her and embraced her. She lowered her head, as if listening attentively, and he kissed her loudly on the neck as she bent down, without interrupting his speech too much. K saw in this the confirmation of the tyranny the student had exercised against him, after the woman's complaints, stood up, and began pacing in the room. He considered how to get rid of the student as quickly as possible, and was glad when the student, apparently disturbed by K's pacing, which had already become a kind of stamping, remarked, "If you're impatient, you can leave. You could have left earlier, nobody would have missed you. In fact, you should have left right away, and quickly." In this remark, it might have expressed all kinds of anger, but certainly also the arrogance of the future civil servant, who was speaking to an obnoxious defendant. K stood close to him and said with a smile, "I am impatient, that's true, but this impatience can be dispelled most easily by you leaving. But perhaps you came to study – I heard you're a student – so I would be happy to make room for you and leave with the woman. You'll have to study much more before you become a judge, however. Although I don't know your court system very well, I assume that just using harsh words, which you know how to wield quite unceremoniously, is not enough." "He shouldn't have been allowed to walk around so freely," said the student, as if explaining K's offensive remarks to the woman, "it was a mistake. I told the investigating judge. At least he should have been kept in his room between interrogations. The investigating judge can be incomprehensible at times." "Empty talk," said K and stretched out his hand towards the woman, "come." "Oh, well," said the student, "no, no, you won't get her," and with a strength not expected of him, he picked her up and ran, bent over, looking affectionately at her, towards the door. A certain fear of K could be discerned here, yet he still dared to provoke him, stroking and pressing the woman's arm with his free hand. K ran a few steps alongside him, ready to grab him and, if necessary, choke him, when the woman said, "It's no use, the investigating judge has me summoned, I can't go with you, this little brat," and she ran her hand over the student's face, "this little brat won't let me." "And you don't want to be freed!" K shouted, and put his hand on the student's shoulder, whereupon the student snapped his teeth at him. "No!" the woman cried and pushed K away with both hands, "no, no, don't do that, what are you thinking! That would be my ruin. Let him go, please, let him go. He's only carrying me to him according to the investigating judge's orders." "Then let him go and I'll never see you again," said K, angry with disappointment, and pushed the student in the back, so that he stumbled briefly, only to spring higher in sheer delight that he had not been refused. K followed them slowly, realizing that this was the first clear defeat he had suffered at their hands. Of course, there was no reason to be scared; he only suffered defeat because he sought out the fight. If he stayed at home and carried on his usual life, he was a thousand times superior to all these people and could clear each one from his path with a single footstep. And he imagined the most ridiculous scene, such as this miserable student, this puffed-up child, this hunched-bearded man kneeling before Elsa's bed and pleading for mercy with clasped hands. K liked this idea so much that he decided, if only for some opportunity, to take the student along to Elsa's one day.
source_text: Nachdem er auf diese Weise die Bedenken gegen die Frau beseitigt hatte, wurde ihm das leise Zwiegespräch am Fenster zu lang, er klopfte mit den Knöcheln auf das Podium und dann auch mit der Faust. Der Student sah kurz über die Schulter der Frau hinweg nach K. hin, ließ sich aber nicht stören, ja drückte sich sogar eng an die Frau und umfaßte sie. Sie senkte tief den Kopf, als höre sie ihm aufmerksam zu, er küßte sie, als sie sich bückte, laut auf den Hals, ohne sich im Reden wesentlich zu unterbrechen. K. sah darin die Tyrannei bestätigt, die der Student nach den klagen der Frau über sie ausübte, stand auf und ging im Zimmer auf und ab. Er überlegte unter Seitenblicken nach dem Studenten, wie er ihn möglichst schnell wegschaffen könnte, und es war ihm daher nicht unwillkommen, als der Student, offenbar gestört durch K.s Herumgehen, das schon zeitweilig zu einem Trampeln ausgeartet war, bemerkte: »Wenn Sie ungeduldig sind, können Sie weggehen. Sie hätten auch schon früher weggehen können, es hätte Sie niemand vermißt. Ja, Sie hätten sogar weggehen sollen, und zwar schon bei meinem Eintritt, und zwar schleunigst.« Es mochte in dieser Bemerkung alle mögliche Wut zum Ausdruck kommen, jedenfalls lag darin aber auch der Hochmut des künftigen Gerichtsbeamten, der zu einem mißliebigen Angeklagten sprach. K. blieb ganz nahe bei ihm stehen und sagte lächelnd: »Ich bin ungeduldig, das ist richtig, aber diese Ungeduld wird am leichtesten dadurch zu beseitigen sein, daß Sie uns verlassen. Wenn Sie aber vielleicht hergekommen sind, um zu studieren – ich hörte, daß Sie Student sind –, so will ich Ihnen gerne Platz machen und mit der Frau weggehen. Sie werden übrigens noch viel studieren müssen, ehe Sie Richter werden. Ich kenne zwar Ihr Gerichtswesen noch nicht sehr genau, nehme aber an, daß es mit groben Reden allein, die Sie allerdings schon unverschämt gut zu führen wissen, noch lange nicht getan ist.« »Man hätte ihn nicht so frei herumlaufen lassen sollen«, sagte der Student, als wolle er der Frau eine Erklärung für K.s beleidigende Rede geben, »es war ein Mißgriff. Ich habe es dem Untersuchungsrichter gesagt. Man hätte ihn zwischen den Verhören zumindest in seinem Zimmer halten sollen. Der Untersuchungsrichter ist manchmal unbegreiflich.« »Unnütze Reden«, sagte K. und streckte die Hand nach der Frau aus, »kommen Sie.« »Ach so«, sagte der Student, »nein, nein, die bekommen Sie nicht«, und mit einer Kraft, die man ihm nicht zugetraut hätte, hob er sie auf einen Arm und lief mit gebeugtem Rücken, zärtlich zu ihr aufsehend, zur Tür. Eine gewisse Angst vor K. war hierbei nicht zu verkennen, trotzdem wagte er es, K. noch zu reizen, indem er mit der freien Hand den Arm der Frau streichelte und drückte. K. lief ein paar Schritte neben ihm her, bereit, ihn zu fassen und, wenn es sein mußte, zu würgen, da sagte die Frau: »Es hilft nichts, der Untersuchungsrichter läßt mich holen, ich darf nicht mit Ihnen gehen, dieses kleine Scheusal«, sie fuhr hierbei dem Studenten mit der Hand übers Gesicht, »dieses kleine Scheusal läßt mich nicht.« »Und Sie wollen nicht befreit werden!« schrie K. und legte die Hand auf die Schulter des Studenten, der mit den Zähnen nach ihr schnappte. »Nein!« rief die Frau und wehrte K. mit beiden Händen ab, »nein, nein, nur das nicht, woran denken Sie denn! Das wäre mein Verderben. Lassen Sie ihn doch, o bitte, lassen Sie ihn doch. Er führt ja nur den Befehl des Untersuchungsrichters aus und trägt mich zu ihm.« »Dann mag er laufen und Sie will ich nie mehr sehen«, sagte K. wütend vor Enttäuschung und gab dem Studenten einen Stoß in den Rücken, daß er kurz stolperte, um gleich darauf, vor Vergnügen darüber, daß er nicht gefallen war, mit seiner Last desto höher zu springen. K. ging ihnen langsam nach, er sah ein, daß das die erste zweifellose Niederlage war, die er von diesen Leuten erfahren hatte. Es war natürlich kein Grund, sich deshalb zu ängstigen, er erhielt die Niederlage nur deshalb, weil er den Kampf aufsuchte. Wenn er zu Hause bliebe und sein gewohntes Leben führte, war er jedem dieser Leute tausendfach überlegen und konnte jeden mit einem Fußtritt von seinem Wege räumen. Und er stellte sich die allerlächerlichste Szene vor, die es zum Beispiel geben würde, wenn dieser klägliche Student, dieses aufgeblasene Kind, dieser krumme Bartträger vor Elsas Bett knien und mit gefalteten Händen um Gnade bitten würde. K. gefiel diese Vorstellung so, daß er beschloß, wenn sich nur irgendeine Gelegenheit dafür ergeben sollte, den Studenten einmal zu Elsa mitzunehmen.

translation: After thus dispelling the concerns about the woman, he found the whispered conversation at the window boring and tapped the podium lightly with his knuckles, and then with his fist. The student looked briefly over the woman's shoulder at K, but was not distracted, indeed, pressed himself even closer to the woman and embraced her. She lowered her head deeply, as if listening attentively, and he kissed her, as she bent down, loudly on the neck, without interrupting his speech too much. K saw his confirmation in the tyranny the student exercised, as described by the woman, and stood up, pacing back and forth in the room. He considered how to get rid of the student as quickly as possible, and he was pleased when the student, apparently disturbed by K’s pacing, which had already turned into stomping, remarked: "If you are impatient, you can leave. You could have left earlier, no one would have missed you. Yes, you should have left, and quickly, as soon as I entered." In this remark, K saw possibly all kinds of anger, but also the arrogance of the future court official, speaking to an undesirable defendant. K stood very close to him and said with a smile, "I am impatient, that is true, but this impatience will be easiest to dispel if you leave us. If perhaps you came to study – I heard that you are a student –, I will willingly make room for you and leave with the woman. You will still have to study a lot more before you become a judge. I may not know your court proceedings very well, but I assume that it is not done solely with rough talk, although you are certainly very good at it." "He should not have been allowed to roam around so freely," said the student, as if explaining to the woman why K’s remarks were offensive, "it was a mistake. I told the investigating judge. He should have been held in the room between interrogations at the very least. The investigating judge can sometimes be incomprehensible." "Useless talk," said K and stretched out his hand toward the woman, "come on." "Oh, I see," said the student, "no, no, you won’t get her," and with a strength not to be expected of him, he lifted her onto his arm and ran with a bent back, looking up affectionately at her, to the door. A certain fear of K was not to be concealed here, but he still dared to tease him by caressing and pressing her arm with his free hand. K ran a few steps beside him, ready to grab him and, if necessary, strangle him, when the woman said, "It’s no use, the investigating judge has me called, I mustn’t go with you, this little devil," she stroked the student’s face with her hand, "this little devil won’t let me." "And you don’t want to be freed!" K shouted and put his hand on the student’s shoulder, on which the student bit down. "No!" the woman cried and pushed K away with both hands, "no, no, not that, what do you think you’re talking about! That would be my ruin. Let him go, oh please, let him go. He’s only carrying me out to the investigating judge to obey his orders." "Then let him go, and I’ll never see you again," said K, enraged by disappointment, and gave the student a shove in the back, causing him to stumble briefly, and then, to his delight that he had not fallen, to jump higher with his load. K followed them slowly, realizing that this was the first unequivocal defeat he had suffered from these people. It was of course no reason to be afraid, he only suffered this defeat because he had sought the fight. If he stayed at home and led his usual life, he was a thousand times superior to each of them and could drive any of them from their path with a single kick. And he imagined the most ridiculous scene, for example, of this pitiful student, this overblown child, this hunchbacked bearded man, kneeling before Elsa’s bed and begging for mercy with folded hands. K liked this idea so much that he decided that if only some opportunity arose, he would take the student to Elsa once.
source_text: Nachdem er auf diese Weise die Bedenken gegen die Frau beseitigt hatte, wurde ihm das leise Zwiegespräch am Fenster zu lang, er klopfte mit den Knöcheln auf das Podium und dann auch mit der Faust. Der Student sah kurz über die Schulter der Frau hinweg nach K. hin, ließ sich aber nicht stören, ja drückte sich sogar eng an die Frau und umfaßte sie. Sie senkte tief den Kopf, als höre sie ihm aufmerksam zu, er küßte sie, als sie sich bückte, laut auf den Hals, ohne sich im Reden wesentlich zu unterbrechen. K. sah darin die Tyrannei bestätigt, die der Student nach den klagen der Frau über sie ausübte, stand auf und ging im Zimmer auf und ab. Er überlegte unter Seitenblicken nach dem Studenten, wie er ihn möglichst schnell wegschaffen könnte, und es war ihm daher nicht unwillkommen, als der Student, offenbar gestört durch K.s Herumgehen, das schon zeitweilig zu einem Trampeln ausgeartet war, bemerkte: »Wenn Sie ungeduldig sind, können Sie weggehen. Sie hätten auch schon früher weggehen können, es hätte Sie niemand vermißt. Ja, Sie hätten sogar weggehen sollen, und zwar schon bei meinem Eintritt, und zwar schleunigst.« Es mochte in dieser Bemerkung alle mögliche Wut zum Ausdruck kommen, jedenfalls lag darin aber auch der Hochmut des künftigen Gerichtsbeamten, der zu einem mißliebigen Angeklagten sprach. K. blieb ganz nahe bei ihm stehen und sagte lächelnd: »Ich bin ungeduldig, das ist richtig, aber diese Ungeduld wird am leichtesten dadurch zu beseitigen sein, daß Sie uns verlassen. Wenn Sie aber vielleicht hergekommen sind, um zu studieren – ich hörte, daß Sie Student sind –, so will ich Ihnen gerne Platz machen und mit der Frau weggehen. Sie werden übrigens noch viel studieren müssen, ehe Sie Richter werden. Ich kenne zwar Ihr Gerichtswesen noch nicht sehr genau, nehme aber an, daß es mit groben Reden allein, die Sie allerdings schon unverschämt gut zu führen wissen, noch lange nicht getan ist.« »Man hätte ihn nicht so frei herumlaufen lassen sollen«, sagte der Student, als wolle er der Frau eine Erklärung für K.s beleidigende Rede geben, »es war ein Mißgriff. Ich habe es dem Untersuchungsrichter gesagt. Man hätte ihn zwischen den Verhören zumindest in seinem Zimmer halten sollen. Der Untersuchungsrichter ist manchmal unbegreiflich.« »Unnütze Reden«, sagte K. und streckte die Hand nach der Frau aus, »kommen Sie.« »Ach so«, sagte der Student, »nein, nein, die bekommen Sie nicht«, und mit einer Kraft, die man ihm nicht zugetraut hätte, hob er sie auf einen Arm und lief mit gebeugtem Rücken, zärtlich zu ihr aufsehend, zur Tür. Eine gewisse Angst vor K. war hierbei nicht zu verkennen, trotzdem wagte er es, K. noch zu reizen, indem er mit der freien Hand den Arm der Frau streichelte und drückte. K. lief ein paar Schritte neben ihm her, bereit, ihn zu fassen und, wenn es sein mußte, zu würgen, da sagte die Frau: »Es hilft nichts, der Untersuchungsrichter läßt mich holen, ich darf nicht mit Ihnen gehen, dieses kleine Scheusal«, sie fuhr hierbei dem Studenten mit der Hand übers Gesicht, »dieses kleine Scheusal läßt mich nicht.« »Und Sie wollen nicht befreit werden!« schrie K. und legte die Hand auf die Schulter des Studenten, der mit den Zähnen nach ihr schnappte. »Nein!« rief die Frau und wehrte K. mit beiden Händen ab, »nein, nein, nur das nicht, woran denken Sie denn! Das wäre mein Verderben. Lassen Sie ihn doch, o bitte, lassen Sie ihn doch. Er führt ja nur den Befehl des Untersuchungsrichters aus und trägt mich zu ihm.« »Dann mag er laufen und Sie will ich nie mehr sehen«, sagte K. wütend vor Enttäuschung und gab dem Studenten einen Stoß in den Rücken, daß er kurz stolperte, um gleich darauf, vor Vergnügen darüber, daß er nicht gefallen war, mit seiner Last desto höher zu springen. K. ging ihnen langsam nach, er sah ein, daß das die erste zweifellose Niederlage war, die er von diesen Leuten erfahren hatte. Es war natürlich kein Grund, sich deshalb zu ängstigen, er erhielt die Niederlage nur deshalb, weil er den Kampf aufsuchte. Wenn er zu Hause bliebe und sein gewohntes Leben führte, war er jedem dieser Leute tausendfach überlegen und konnte jeden mit einem Fußtritt von seinem Wege räumen. Und er stellte sich die allerlächerlichste Szene vor, die es zum Beispiel geben würde, wenn dieser klägliche Student, dieses aufgeblasene Kind, dieser krumme Bartträger vor Elsas Bett knien und mit gefalteten Händen um Gnade bitten würde. K. gefiel diese Vorstellung so, daß er beschloß, wenn sich nur irgendeine Gelegenheit dafür ergeben sollte, den Studenten einmal zu Elsa mitzunehmen.

translation: After he had thus dispelled the reservations about the woman, he found the whispered conversation by the window tedious, and rapped on the lectern first with his knuckles, then with his fist. The student briefly glanced over the woman’s shoulder towards K., but was not disturbed, and even pressed himself closer to her and embraced her. She lowered her head deeply, as if listening attentively, and he kissed her on the neck, when she bent down, loudly, without interrupting his speech much. K. saw in this the confirmation of the tyranny to which the student subjected her according to the woman’s complaints, stood up, and began pacing in the room. With sideways glances at the student, he pondered how to get rid of him as quickly as possible, and he was glad when the student, apparently annoyed by K.’s pacing, which had already turned into trampling, remarked, "If you are impatient, you can leave. You could have left earlier, nobody would have missed you. In fact, you should have left right away, immediately, when I came in." There might be all kinds of anger in this remark, but certainly there was also the arrogance of the future judicial officer speaking to an unwelcome defendant. K. stood very close to him and said with a smile, "I am indeed impatient, that is correct, but this impatience can be easily remedied by your leaving. But perhaps you came here to study – I heard that you are a student –, in which case I would gladly make room for you and go away with the woman. You will have to study much more before you become a judge. Although I do not know your judicial proceedings very well, I assume that it is not sufficient to use coarse words, which you know how to use rather unscrupulously." "He shouldn’t have been allowed to walk around so freely," said the student, as if explaining K.’s offensive speech to the woman, "it was a mistake. I told the examining magistrate. At the very least, he should have been kept in his room during the interrogations. The examining magistrate can be quite incomprehensible sometimes." "Useless words," said K., and stretched out his hand towards the woman, "come on." "Oh, so," said the student, "no, no, you won’t get her," and with a strength that was not to be expected of him, he lifted her onto one arm and ran with his back bent, looking lovingly up at her, to the door. A certain fear of K. could not be denied, yet he still dared to provoke him by caressing and pressing the woman’s arm with his free hand. K. ran a few steps alongside him, ready to grab him and strangle him if necessary, when the woman said, "It’s no use, the examining magistrate is going to fetch me, I can’t go with you, you little devil," she patted the student’s face with her hand, "you little devil won’t let me." "And you don’t want to be released!" shouted K., and laid his hand on the student’s shoulder, whom he bit. "No!" cried the woman and pushed K. away with both hands, "no, no, not that, what are you thinking of! That would be my ruin. Let him go, oh please, let him go. He is only carrying me out of obedience to the examining magistrate’s orders." "Then he can go and I will never see you again," said K. in anger, and pushed the student in the back, so that he stumbled for a moment, then leaped even higher with his burden in sheer joy at not having fallen. K. followed them slowly, realizing that this was the first unmistakable defeat he had suffered at the hands of these people. Of course, there was no reason to be afraid because he only sought the fight. If he stayed at home and led his usual life, he was a thousand times superior to each of these people and could drive any of them off his path with a single kick. And he imagined the most absurd scene, for example, this pitiful student, this puffed-up child, this crooked-bearded man kneeling in front of Elsa’s bed with his hands folded, begging for mercy. K. liked this vision so much that he decided that if only some opportunity arose, he would take the student to Elsa with him.
source_text: Nachdem er auf diese Weise die Bedenken gegen die Frau beseitigt hatte, wurde ihm das leise Zwiegespräch am Fenster zu lang, er klopfte mit den Knöcheln auf das Podium und dann auch mit der Faust. Der Student sah kurz über die Schulter der Frau hinweg nach K. hin, ließ sich aber nicht stören, ja drückte sich sogar eng an die Frau und umfaßte sie. Sie senkte tief den Kopf, als höre sie ihm aufmerksam zu, er küßte sie, als sie sich bückte, laut auf den Hals, ohne sich im Reden wesentlich zu unterbrechen. K. sah darin die Tyrannei bestätigt, die der Student nach den klagen der Frau über sie ausübte, stand auf und ging im Zimmer auf und ab. Er überlegte unter Seitenblicken nach dem Studenten, wie er ihn möglichst schnell wegschaffen könnte, und es war ihm daher nicht unwillkommen, als der Student, offenbar gestört durch K.s Herumgehen, das schon zeitweilig zu einem Trampeln ausgeartet war, bemerkte: »Wenn Sie ungeduldig sind, können Sie weggehen. Sie hätten auch schon früher weggehen können, es hätte Sie niemand vermißt. Ja, Sie hätten sogar weggehen sollen, und zwar schon bei meinem Eintritt, und zwar schleunigst.« Es mochte in dieser Bemerkung alle mögliche Wut zum Ausdruck kommen, jedenfalls lag darin aber auch der Hochmut des künftigen Gerichtsbeamten, der zu einem mißliebigen Angeklagten sprach. K. blieb ganz nahe bei ihm stehen und sagte lächelnd: »Ich bin ungeduldig, das ist richtig, aber diese Ungeduld wird am leichtesten dadurch zu beseitigen sein, daß Sie uns verlassen. Wenn Sie aber vielleicht hergekommen sind, um zu studieren – ich hörte, daß Sie Student sind –, so will ich Ihnen gerne Platz machen und mit der Frau weggehen. Sie werden übrigens noch viel studieren müssen, ehe Sie Richter werden. Ich kenne zwar Ihr Gerichtswesen noch nicht sehr genau, nehme aber an, daß es mit groben Reden allein, die Sie allerdings schon unverschämt gut zu führen wissen, noch lange nicht getan ist.« »Man hätte ihn nicht so frei herumlaufen lassen sollen«, sagte der Student, als wolle er der Frau eine Erklärung für K.s beleidigende Rede geben, »es war ein Mißgriff. Ich habe es dem Untersuchungsrichter gesagt. Man hätte ihn zwischen den Verhören zumindest in seinem Zimmer halten sollen. Der Untersuchungsrichter ist manchmal unbegreiflich.« »Unnütze Reden«, sagte K. und streckte die Hand nach der Frau aus, »kommen Sie.« »Ach so«, sagte der Student, »nein, nein, die bekommen Sie nicht«, und mit einer Kraft, die man ihm nicht zugetraut hätte, hob er sie auf einen Arm und lief mit gebeugtem Rücken, zärtlich zu ihr aufsehend, zur Tür. Eine gewisse Angst vor K. war hierbei nicht zu verkennen, trotzdem wagte er es, K. noch zu reizen, indem er mit der freien Hand den Arm der Frau streichelte und drückte. K. lief ein paar Schritte neben ihm her, bereit, ihn zu fassen und, wenn es sein mußte, zu würgen, da sagte die Frau: »Es hilft nichts, der Untersuchungsrichter läßt mich holen, ich darf nicht mit Ihnen gehen, dieses kleine Scheusal«, sie fuhr hierbei dem Studenten mit der Hand übers Gesicht, »dieses kleine Scheusal läßt mich nicht.« »Und Sie wollen nicht befreit werden!« schrie K. und legte die Hand auf die Schulter des Studenten, der mit den Zähnen nach ihr schnappte. »Nein!« rief die Frau und wehrte K. mit beiden Händen ab, »nein, nein, nur das nicht, woran denken Sie denn! Das wäre mein Verderben. Lassen Sie ihn doch, o bitte, lassen Sie ihn doch. Er führt ja nur den Befehl des Untersuchungsrichters aus und trägt mich zu ihm.« »Dann mag er laufen und Sie will ich nie mehr sehen«, sagte K. wütend vor Enttäuschung und gab dem Studenten einen Stoß in den Rücken, daß er kurz stolperte, um gleich darauf, vor Vergnügen darüber, daß er nicht gefallen war, mit seiner Last desto höher zu springen. K. ging ihnen langsam nach, er sah ein, daß das die erste zweifellose Niederlage war, die er von diesen Leuten erfahren hatte. Es war natürlich kein Grund, sich deshalb zu ängstigen, er erhielt die Niederlage nur deshalb, weil er den Kampf aufsuchte. Wenn er zu Hause bliebe und sein gewohntes Leben führte, war er jedem dieser Leute tausendfach überlegen und konnte jeden mit einem Fußtritt von seinem Wege räumen. Und er stellte sich die allerlächerlichste Szene vor, die es zum Beispiel geben würde, wenn dieser klägliche Student, dieses aufgeblasene Kind, dieser krumme Bartträger vor Elsas Bett knien und mit gefalteten Händen um Gnade bitten würde. K. gefiel diese Vorstellung so, daß er beschloß, wenn sich nur irgendeine Gelegenheit dafür ergeben sollte, den Studenten einmal zu Elsa mitzunehmen.

translation: After he had dispelled her misgivings about him, he found the low murmurings by the window too tedious, and he tapped on the table with his knuckles, and then with his fist. The student glanced over the woman’s shoulder toward K, but wasn’t perturbed, nor did he shy away; on the contrary, he pressed himself even closer to the woman and clasped her. She lowered her head deep, as if listening attentively, and kissed her as she bent down, loudly on the neck, without interrupting his speech much. K. saw in this the confirmation of the tyranny which the student had been exercising on him after the woman’s complaints about him, stood up, and began pacing back and forth in the room. He considered how to get rid of the student as quickly as possible and was glad that the student, apparently annoyed by K.’s pacing, which had already degenerated into stamping, remarked: "If you are impatient, you can leave. You could have left much earlier; no one would have missed you. In fact, you should have left the moment I came in, and quickly. " There might have been various sorts of rage in that remark, but certainly, there was also the pride of the future public servant, who was speaking to an undesirable defendant. K. stood very close to him and said with a smile: "I am impatient, that is true, but this impatience will be most easily remedied by your departure. But perhaps you came here to study— I heard that you are a student—then I will gladly make room for you and go with the woman. You will, however, have to study much more before you become a judge. Although I am not very familiar with your judicial practices, I assume that they cannot be carried out by merely making coarse remarks, which you know how to make rather unashamedly well." "He shouldn’t have been allowed to roam around so freely," the student said, as if explaining K.’s offensive remarks to the woman, "it was a mistake. I have told the investigating judge. He should at least have been kept in his room between interrogations. The investigating judge can be inexplicable at times." "Idle talk," said K. and stretched out his hand toward the woman, "come along." "Oh, so," said the student, "no, no, you won’t get her," and with a strength that seemed surprising, he lifted her onto his arm and ran with his back bent, looking tenderly at her, to the door. A certain fear of K. could be discerned here, but he still dared to provoke K., by caressing and pressing the woman’s arm with his free hand. K. ran a few steps beside him, ready to grab him and choke him if necessary, but as the woman said: "It’s no use, the investigating judge will have me, I cannot go with you, this little brat," she stroked the student’s face here, "this little brat won’t let me." "And you don’t want to be freed!" K. shouted and put his hand on the student’s shoulder, who snapped at her with his teeth. "No!" the woman cried and pushed K. away with both hands, "no, no, not that, what are you thinking of! That would be my ruin. Let him go, oh please, let him go. He is only carrying me out on the investigating judge’s orders." "Then let him run, I will never see you again," said K. in anger and pushed the student in the back, causing him to stumble for a moment, before he jumped even higher with his burden out of sheer delight at the fact that he had not fallen. K. followed them slowly, realizing that this was the first clear defeat he had suffered at the hands of these people. Of course, there was no reason to be afraid of this; he was merely accepting the defeat because he had sought the fight. If he stayed at home and continued his usual life, he was a thousand times better than all of them and could easily clear any of them from his path with a kick. And he imagined the most ridiculous scene, for example, that pitiful student, this inflated child, this crooked-bearded man, would kneel before Elsa’s bed and beg for mercy with his hands folded. K. liked this idea so much that he decided that if any such opportunity presented itself, he would take the student to Elsa once.
source_text: Nachdem er auf diese Weise die Bedenken gegen die Frau beseitigt hatte, wurde ihm das leise Zwiegespräch am Fenster zu lang, er klopfte mit den Knöcheln auf das Podium und dann auch mit der Faust. Der Student sah kurz über die Schulter der Frau hinweg nach K. hin, ließ sich aber nicht stören, ja drückte sich sogar eng an die Frau und umfaßte sie. Sie senkte tief den Kopf, als höre sie ihm aufmerksam zu, er küßte sie, als sie sich bückte, laut auf den Hals, ohne sich im Reden wesentlich zu unterbrechen. K. sah darin die Tyrannei bestätigt, die der Student nach den klagen der Frau über sie ausübte, stand auf und ging im Zimmer auf und ab. Er überlegte unter Seitenblicken nach dem Studenten, wie er ihn möglichst schnell wegschaffen könnte, und es war ihm daher nicht unwillkommen, als der Student, offenbar gestört durch K.s Herumgehen, das schon zeitweilig zu einem Trampeln ausgeartet war, bemerkte: »Wenn Sie ungeduldig sind, können Sie weggehen. Sie hätten auch schon früher weggehen können, es hätte Sie niemand vermißt. Ja, Sie hätten sogar weggehen sollen, und zwar schon bei meinem Eintritt, und zwar schleunigst.« Es mochte in dieser Bemerkung alle mögliche Wut zum Ausdruck kommen, jedenfalls lag darin aber auch der Hochmut des künftigen Gerichtsbeamten, der zu einem mißliebigen Angeklagten sprach. K. blieb ganz nahe bei ihm stehen und sagte lächelnd: »Ich bin ungeduldig, das ist richtig, aber diese Ungeduld wird am leichtesten dadurch zu beseitigen sein, daß Sie uns verlassen. Wenn Sie aber vielleicht hergekommen sind, um zu studieren – ich hörte, daß Sie Student sind –, so will ich Ihnen gerne Platz machen und mit der Frau weggehen. Sie werden übrigens noch viel studieren müssen, ehe Sie Richter werden. Ich kenne zwar Ihr Gerichtswesen noch nicht sehr genau, nehme aber an, daß es mit groben Reden allein, die Sie allerdings schon unverschämt gut zu führen wissen, noch lange nicht getan ist.« »Man hätte ihn nicht so frei herumlaufen lassen sollen«, sagte der Student, als wolle er der Frau eine Erklärung für K.s beleidigende Rede geben, »es war ein Mißgriff. Ich habe es dem Untersuchungsrichter gesagt. Man hätte ihn zwischen den Verhören zumindest in seinem Zimmer halten sollen. Der Untersuchungsrichter ist manchmal unbegreiflich.« »Unnütze Reden«, sagte K. und streckte die Hand nach der Frau aus, »kommen Sie.« »Ach so«, sagte der Student, »nein, nein, die bekommen Sie nicht«, und mit einer Kraft, die man ihm nicht zugetraut hätte, hob er sie auf einen Arm und lief mit gebeugtem Rücken, zärtlich zu ihr aufsehend, zur Tür. Eine gewisse Angst vor K. war hierbei nicht zu verkennen, trotzdem wagte er es, K. noch zu reizen, indem er mit der freien Hand den Arm der Frau streichelte und drückte. K. lief ein paar Schritte neben ihm her, bereit, ihn zu fassen und, wenn es sein mußte, zu würgen, da sagte die Frau: »Es hilft nichts, der Untersuchungsrichter läßt mich holen, ich darf nicht mit Ihnen gehen, dieses kleine Scheusal«, sie fuhr hierbei dem Studenten mit der Hand übers Gesicht, »dieses kleine Scheusal läßt mich nicht.« »Und Sie wollen nicht befreit werden!« schrie K. und legte die Hand auf die Schulter des Studenten, der mit den Zähnen nach ihr schnappte. »Nein!« rief die Frau und wehrte K. mit beiden Händen ab, »nein, nein, nur das nicht, woran denken Sie denn! Das wäre mein Verderben. Lassen Sie ihn doch, o bitte, lassen Sie ihn doch. Er führt ja nur den Befehl des Untersuchungsrichters aus und trägt mich zu ihm.« »Dann mag er laufen und Sie will ich nie mehr sehen«, sagte K. wütend vor Enttäuschung und gab dem Studenten einen Stoß in den Rücken, daß er kurz stolperte, um gleich darauf, vor Vergnügen darüber, daß er nicht gefallen war, mit seiner Last desto höher zu springen. K. ging ihnen langsam nach, er sah ein, daß das die erste zweifellose Niederlage war, die er von diesen Leuten erfahren hatte. Es war natürlich kein Grund, sich deshalb zu ängstigen, er erhielt die Niederlage nur deshalb, weil er den Kampf aufsuchte. Wenn er zu Hause bliebe und sein gewohntes Leben führte, war er jedem dieser Leute tausendfach überlegen und konnte jeden mit einem Fußtritt von seinem Wege räumen. Und er stellte sich die allerlächerlichste Szene vor, die es zum Beispiel geben würde, wenn dieser klägliche Student, dieses aufgeblasene Kind, dieser krumme Bartträger vor Elsas Bett knien und mit gefalteten Händen um Gnade bitten würde. K. gefiel diese Vorstellung so, daß er beschloß, wenn sich nur irgendeine Gelegenheit dafür ergeben sollte, den Studenten einmal zu Elsa mitzunehmen.

translation: —"Didn't you both claim neither to me nor to him?" Aglaya cried. "And what about your letters? Who asked you to meddle in our matters and persuade me to marry him? Is that not a claim? Why do you persist in coming to us? At first I thought you wished to disgust me with him by getting yourself involved and making me give him up, and only later did I realize what you were after: you simply imagined that you were performing some noble deed by all this posturing... How could you possibly love him when you love your vanity so much? Why didn't you simply leave and not waste time writing those silly letters? Why don't you marry now some noble man who loves you so and has honored you by offering his hand? The reason is too obvious: if you marry Rogozhin, what kind of resentment would be left? You would even be too well off! Eugene Pavlovich said you read too many poems and that you are 'too educated for your station'; that you are a bookish woman and a white-collar girl; add to that your vanity, and that is the whole sum of your reasons... "
source_text: — Как не заявляли «ни ему, ни мне»? — вскричала Аглая. — А письма-то ваши? Кто вас просил нас сватать и меня уговаривать идти за него? Разве это не заявление? Зачем вы к нам напрашиваетесь? Я сначала было подумала, что вы хотите, напротив, отвращение во мне к нему поселить тем, что к нам замешались, и чтоб я его бросила, и потом только догадалась, в чем дело: вам просто вообразилось, что вы высокий подвиг делаете всеми этими кривляниями... Ну могли ли вы его любить, если так любите свое тщеславие? Зачем вы просто не уехали отсюда, вместо того чтобы мне смешные письма писать? Зачем вы не выходите теперь за благородного человека, который вас так любит и сделал вам честь, предложив свою руку? Слишком ясно зачем: выйдете за Рогожина, какая же тогда обида останется? Даже слишком уж много чести получите! Про вас Евгений Павлыч сказал, что вы слишком много поэм прочли и «слишком много образованны для вашего... положения»; что вы книжная женщина и белоручка; прибавьте ваше тщеславие, вот и все ваши причины...
gt_translation: - How did they not say “neither to him, nor to me”? cried Aglaya. What about your letters? Who asked you to marry us and persuade me to marry him? Isn't this a statement? Why are you asking us? At first I thought that you wanted, on the contrary, to plant disgust in me for him by getting mixed up with us, and so that I would leave him, and then I only guessed what was the matter: you just imagined that you were doing a high feat with all these antics ... Well, could you love him, if you love your vanity so much? Why didn't you just leave here instead of writing funny letters to me? Why don't you now marry a noble man who loves you so much and has done you the honor of offering his hand? It is too clear why: if you marry Rogozhin, then what kind of resentment will remain? Even get too much honor! Yevgeny Pavlich said about you that you have read too many poems and "are too educated for your ... position"; that you are a bookish woman and a white hand; add your vanity, that's all your reasons...

human_translations.translator_1: “What do you mean you didn’t say anything to me or to him?” Aglaya exclaimed. “What about your letters? Who asked you to be our go-between and try to persuade me to marry him? Isn’t that enough? Why are you foisting yourself upon us? At first I had, on the contrary, the impression that by your answer you meant to set me up against him and that I should leave him. It was only later I realized what was going on. You imagine you’re making some noble sacrifice with all this posturing… Could one whose first love is vanity possibly love him? Why didn’t you simply go away, instead of writing these ridiculous letters to me? Why don’t you marry a respectable gentleman, who loves you so much and has honoured you with offering you his hand? The reason is all too obvious. If you were to marry Rogozhin, where would be your sense of having been hurt? He’d be doing you too much of an honour anyway. Yevgeny Pavlovich said about you that you’ve read too much poetry and that you’re too educated for your… station, that you’re bookish and indolent. Add vanity to it, and it all becomes clear—”

human_translations.translator_3: “I have never declared either to him or to you that I love him,” Nastasya Filippovna spoke with effort, “and … you’re right, I ran away from him …” she added barely audibly. “What do you mean you ‘never declared either to him or to me’?” cried Aglaya. “And what about your letters? At first I thought you wanted, on the contrary, to make me loathe him by meddling with us, so that I would abandon him, and only later did I guess what it was: you simply imagined that you were doing a lofty deed with all this posturing … Well, how could you love him, if you love your vanity so much? Why didn’t you simply go away, instead of writing ridiculous letters to me? Why don’t you now marry the noble man who loves you so much and has honored you by offering his hand? It’s all too clear why: if you marry Rogozhin, what sort of offense will you have left then? You’ll even get too much honor! Evgeny Pavlych said of you that you’ve read too many poems and are ‘too well educated for your … position’; that you’re a bookish woman and a lily-white; add your vanity, and there are all your reasons …”
human_translations.translator_4: "Never told either him or me?" cried Aglaya. "How about your letters? Who asked you to try to persuade me to marry him? Was not that a declaration from you? Why do you force yourself upon us in this way? I confess I thought at first that you were anxious to arouse an aversion for him in my heart by your meddling, in order that I might give him up; and it was only afterwards that I guessed the truth. You imagined that you were doing an heroic action! How could you spare any love for him, when you love your own vanity to such an extent? Why could you not simply go away from here, instead of writing me those absurd letters? Why do you not NOW marry that generous man who loves you, and has done you the honour of offering you his hand? It is plain enough why; if you marry Rogojin you lose your grievance; you will have nothing more to complain of. You will be receiving too much honour. Evgenie Pavlovitch was saying the other day that you had read too many poems and are too well educated for—your position; and that you live in idleness. Add to this your vanity, and, there you have reason enough—"

translation: The words of farewell still linger in my ears, yet in a moment I find myself facing the Eastern Sea." With this, the Monkey King pressed down his cloud and arrived at Flower and Fruit Mountain. Following the path, he suddenly heard cranes crying and monkeys howling. The cries of the cranes soared into the heavens, while the mournful cries of the monkeys were heart-rending. Monkey King immediately called out, "Children, I have returned!" From beneath the cliffs, around the flowers and grass, and among the trees, both large and small monkeys leapt out, numbering in the thousands, surrounding the Handsome Monkey King and bowing, calling, "Great King, you have been so kind! Why have you been away for so long? You have left us all waiting, as if we were dying of thirst and famine! Lately, a demon has been oppressing us, forcing us to cede control of our Water Curtain Cave. We have fought bravely, but he has taken our belongings and captured many of our kin, leaving us sleepless day and night to guard our home. Thankfully, Great King, you have returned! If you do not come for another year, we may all be the demon's subjects!" Hearing this, Monkey King's heart filled with rage. "What demon dares to act thus? Tell me in detail, so I may find him and take revenge." The monkeys all fell to their knees and cried, "O Great King, this demon calls himself the World-Reversing Demon King, and he resides to the north." Monkey King asked, "How far is it from here to his lair?" The monkeys replied, "He comes in mist and goes in clouds, with wind, rain, thunder, and lightning. We cannot tell how far it is." Monkey King said, "In that case, do not fear. Go and amuse yourselves, while I go and find him!"
source_text: 别语叮咛还在耳，何期顷刻见东溟。”悟空按下云头，直至花果山。找路而走，忽听得鹤唳猿啼，鹤唳声冲霄汉外，猿啼悲切甚伤情。即开口叫道：“孩儿们，我来了也！”那崖下石坎边，花草中，树木里，若大若小之猴，跳出千千万万，把个美猴王围在当中，叩头叫道：“大王，你好宽心！怎么一去许久？把我们俱闪在这里，望你诚如饥渴！近来被一妖魔在此欺虐，强要占我们水帘洞府，是我等舍死忘生，与他争斗。这些时，被那厮抢了我们家火，捉了许多子侄，教我们昼夜无眠，看守家业。幸得大王来了！大王若再年载不来，我等连山洞尽属他人矣！”悟空闻说，心中大怒道：“是甚么妖魔，辄敢无状！你且细细说来，待我寻他报仇。”众猴叩头：“告上大王，那厮自称混世魔王，住居在直北下。”悟空道：“此间到他那里，有多少路程？”众猴道：“他来时云，去时雾，或风或雨，或雷或电，我等不知有多少路。”悟空道：“既如此，你们休怕，且自顽耍，等我寻他去来！”

He was looking for a way to go, and suddenly he heard the chirping of cranes and chirps. and also! Why did you go for a long time? Flash us all here, I hope you are as hungry as you are! Recently, I was bullied here by a demon, who forcibly took over our Shuilian Cave Mansion. At these times, the fellow robbed our family of fire, captured many sons and nephews, taught us sleepless nights and nights, and guarded the family business. Fortunately, the king is here! If the king does not come again in the next year, even the cave will belong to someone else! When Wukong heard that, he was furious in his heart: "What kind of monster, you dare to be invisible!" Tell me in detail, until I seek his revenge. All the monkeys kowtowed: "Speak to the king, that fellow calls himself the Demon King of Confusion, and lives in Zhibeixia." Wukong said: "How long is the distance from here to him?" "The monkeys said: "When he comes, it is cloudy, and when he leaves, it is foggy, whether it is wind or rain, whether it is thunder or lightning, I don't know how many roads there are. "Wukong said: "Since that's the case, don't be afraid, and play with yourselves, wait for me to find him!" "

human_translations.translator_1: Words of farewell still echo in my ears. I ne’er hope to see so soon the eastern depths!” Wukong lowered the direction of his cloud and landed squarely on the Flower-Fruit Mountain. He was trying to find his way when he heard the call of cranes and the cry of monkeys; the call of cranes reverberated in the Heavens, and the cry of monkeys moved his spirit with sadness. “Little ones,” he called out, “I have returned!” From the crannies of the cliff, from the flowers and bushes, and from the woods and trees, monkeys great and small leaped out by the tens of thousands and surrounded the Handsome Monkey King. They all kowtowed and cried, “Great King! What laxity of mind! Why did you go away for such a long time and leave us here longing for your return like someone hungering and thirsting? Recently, we have been brutally abused by a monster, who wanted to rob us of our Water-Curtain Cave. Out of sheer desperation, we fought hard with him. And yet all this time, that fellow has plundered many of our possessions, kidnapped a number of our young ones, and given us many restless days and nights watching over our property. How fortunate that our great king has returned! If the great king had stayed away another year or so, we and the entire mountain cave would have belonged to someone else!” Hearing this, Wukong was filled with anger. “What sort of a monster is this,” he cried, “that behaves in such a lawless manner? Tell me in detail and I will find him to exact vengeance.” “Be informed, Great King,” the monkeys said, kowtowing, “that the fellow calls himself the Monstrous King of Havoc, and he lives north of here.” Wukong asked, “From here to his place, how great is the distance?” The monkeys replied, “He comes like the cloud and leaves like the mist, like the wind and the rain, like lightning and thunder. We don’t know how great the distance is.” “In that case,” said Wukong, “go and play for a while and don’t be afraid. Let me go and find him.”
human_translations.translator_2: Finally the Seeker of Secrets descended safely from the clouds, arrived at the Mountain Garden and there heard the monkeys crying bitterly. He said, “My children, I have returned, what is the matter?” Ten thousand monkeys, great and small, ran towards him from all the rocks and trees about, knelt before him and cried, “Why did you leave us so long here without protection? We have been longing for your return like men who are hungry and thirsty. Of late we have been troubled by the Chief Disturber of the World’s Peace, who wanted to take possession of our cave by force. We fought him at the risk of our lives and many were killed. If you, Oh King, had not returned, there would soon have been no cave left us at all.” The Seeker of Secrets became very angry and asked what evil spirit it was that had dared do that. “We will soon have our revenge on him. Where does he live and how far away?” “We do not know. He came with the wind and went away in a fog.” At this the Seeker of Secrets said, “I will find him.”
human_translations.translator_3: Just as he was trying to work out which path to take back to Water-Curtain Cave, he heard the cries of cranes and monkeys echoing about him. “I’m back, little ones!” he called. From out of rocky enclaves, grasses, flowers, and trees, thousands of monkeys of different sizes leaped out and surrounded their king. “Why were you gone so long? A cruel demon has attacked Water-Curtain Cave, stolen our possessions, and kidnapped our children.” “Who is this insolent fiend?” raged Monkey. “Tell me everything, and I’ll settle his hash.” “He calls himself the Monstrous King of Chaos, and he lives north of here.” “How far?” “We don’t know. He arrives like the clouds and departs like the mist, wind, rain, thunder, and lightning.” “Very well.
human_translations.translator_4: The parting words still echo in my ears; When will I see The Eastern Ocean again?” Sun Wukong put away his cloud and headed straight to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit. As he followed the path there he heard the call of the cranes and the cries of the apes. The crane calls echoed beyond the Milky Way, and the ape cries were pathetically sad. Sun Wukong shouted, “Children, I'm back.” Big monkeys and little monkeys came bounding in their thousands and tens of thousands from caves in the cliffs, from the grass and flowers, and down from the trees. They all crowded round the Handsome Monkey King, kowtowed and said, “Your Majesty, you're a cool one. How could you stay away for so long, abandoning us all here? We've been desperate for you to come back. A demon has been mistreating us terribly. He's occupied our Water Curtain Cave, and we've been fighting for our lives with him. Recently he's been stealing our things and carrying off many of our youngsters. We've had to stay awake all night to guard our families. Thank goodness you've come back! Another year without you, Your Majesty, and every one of us would be under his control, cave and all.” Sun Wukong was furious, “Who is this demon? What an outrage! Tell me everything about him, and then I'll go and give him what's coming to him.” The monkey host kowtowed again and said, “Your Majesty, the wretch calls himself the Demon King of Confusion. He lives North of here.” “How far away is his lair?” Sun Wukong asked. “He comes and goes in cloud and mist with wind and rain, or thunder and lightning, so we don't know how far it is.” “If that's how it is,” Sun Wukong replied, “then don't worry. Just keep yourselves amused while I go and find him.”

translation: The parting words still linger in my ears; how unexpected to see the Eastern Sea in an instant.” With that, the Monkey King brought his cloud to a halt and arrived at Flower and Fruit Mountain. He followed the path, and suddenly heard the cries of cranes and the wails of monkeys. The cry of the crane pierced the heavens, while the wail of the monkey was filled with sorrow and pain. He called out, “Children, I am here!” Instantly, countless monkeys of all sizes leaped out from the cliffs, flowers, and trees, surrounding the Handsome Monkey King, bowing and calling out, “Great King, how can you have such peace of mind! Why have you been gone for so long, leaving us all behind? We have long yearned for your return, like a parched land awaiting rain! Lately, a demon has been tormenting us, forcing his way into our Water Curtain Cave. It was only through our deaths and dangers that we could resist him. For these past days, he has taken our family treasures, captured many of our kin, and has kept us awake day and night to guard our property. Fortunately, the great king has returned! If you do not return for another year, we shall have lost our mountain and cave to others!” The Monkey King, upon hearing this, was filled with rage and said, “What demon dares to act so outrageously! The parting words still resounded in my ears, yet in a moment I found myself before the Eastern Sea. With a wave of his hand, Sun Wukong alighted and arrived at Flower and Fruit Mountain. Searching for a path, he suddenly heard the cries of cranes and the howls of apes. The cries of the cranes soared beyond the clouds, while the howls of the apes were full of sorrow, stirring deep emotions. Sun Wukong called out, "Children, I have come!" Instantly, countless monkeys of various sizes leaped out from the rocks, bushes, and trees, surrounding their beautiful king and prostrating themselves, calling out, "Your Majesty, how could you leave us so long? We have been left here, longing for you as one would hunger for food! Lately, a demon has been bullying us and forcefully taking our Water Curtain Cave. We have fought to the death to protect our home, but he has taken our fire and captured many of our kin, leaving us without rest day and night, guarding our property. We are grateful that your Majesty has returned! If you do not return for another year, we will be left with nothing!"

Sun Wukong, hearing this, was greatly angered and said, "What demon dares to act so impudently! Speak to me in detail so that I may seek revenge." The monkeys prostrated themselves, saying, "Your Majesty, this demon calls himself the Devil King of the World and resides to the north of us." Sun Wukong asked, "How far is it to his lair from here?" The monkeys replied, "He comes and goes in the form of clouds and mists, sometimes as wind, sometimes as rain, sometimes as thunder, and sometimes as lightning. We do not know how many miles it is." Sun Wukong said, "If that is so, do not be afraid. Play about and wait for me to find him."
