human_translations.translator_4: As usual, there was at first no response to K.'s ring at the door. "Leni could be a bit quicker," thought K. But he could at least be glad there was nobody else interfering as usually happened, be it the man in his nightshirt or anyone else who might bother him. As K. pressed on the button for the second time he looked back at the other door, but this time it, too, remained closed. At last, two eyes appeared at the spy-hatch in the lawyer's door, although they weren't Leni's eyes. Someone unlocked the door, but kept himself pressed against it as he called back inside, "It's him!", and only then did he open the door properly. K. pushed against the door, as behind him he could already hear the key being hurriedly turned in the lock of the door to the other flat. When the door in front of him finally opened, he stormed straight into the hallway. Through the corridor which led between the rooms he saw Leni, to whom the warning cry of the door opener had been directed, still running away in her nightshirt. He looked at her for a moment and then looked round at the person who had opened the door. It was a small, wizened man with a full beard, he held a candle in his hand. "Do you work here? " asked K. " No," answered the man, "I don't belong here at all, the lawyer is only representing me, I'm here on legal business." "Without your coat?" asked K., indicating the man's deficiency of dress with a gesture of his hand. "Oh, do forgive me!" said the man, and he looked at himself in the light of the candle he was holding as if he had not known about his appearance until then. "Is Leni your lover? " asked K. curtly. He had set his legs slightly apart, his hands, in which he held his hat, were behind his back. Merely by being in possession of a thick overcoat he felt his advantage over this thin little man. " Oh God," he said and, shocked, raised one hand in front of his face as if in defence, "no, no, what can you be thinking?" "You look honest enough," said K. with a smile, "but come along anyway. " K. indicated with his hat which way the man was to go and let him go ahead of him. "What is your name then?" asked K. on the way. " Block. I'm a businessman," said the small man, twisting himself round as he thus introduced himself, although K. did not allow him to stop moving. "Is that your real name?" asked K. "Of course it is," was the man's reply, "why do you doubt it?" "I thought you might have some reason to keep your name secret," said K. He felt himself as much at liberty as is normally only felt in foreign parts when speaking with people of lower standing, keeping everything about himself to himself, speaking only casually about the interests of the other, able to raise him to a level above one's own, but also able, at will, to let him drop again. K. stopped at the door of the lawyer's office, opened it and, to the businessman who had obediently gone ahead, called, "Not so fast! Bring some light here!" K. thought Leni might have hidden in here, he let the businessman search in every corner, but the room was empty. In front of the picture of the judge K. took hold of the businessman's braces to stop him moving on. " Do you know him?" he asked, pointing upwards with his finger. The businessman lifted the candle, blinked as he looked up and said, "It's a judge." "An important judge?" asked K., and stood to the side and in front of the businessman so that he could observe what impression the picture had on him. The businessman was looking up in admiration. " He's an important judge." "You don't have much insight," said K. " He is the lowest of the lowest examining judges." "I remember now," said the businessman as he lowered the candle, "that's what I've already been told." "Well of course you have," called out K., "I'd forgotten about it, of course you would already have been told." "But why, why?" asked the businessman as he moved forwards towards the door, propelled by the hands of K. Outside in the corridor K. said, "You know where Leni's hidden, do you?" "Hidden?" said the businessman, "No, but she might be in the kitchen cooking soup for the lawyer." "Why didn't you say that immediately?" asked K. "I was going to take you there, but you called me back again," answered the businessman, as if confused by the contradictory commands. "You think you're very clever, don't you," said K, "now take me there!" K. had never been in the kitchen, it was surprisingly big and very well equipped. The stove alone was three times bigger than normal stoves, but it was not possible to see any detail beyond this as the kitchen was at the time illuminated by no more than a small lamp hanging by the entrance. At the stove stood Leni, in a white apron as always, breaking eggs into a pot standing on a spirit lamp. " Good evening, Josef," she said with a glance sideways. " Good evening," said K., pointing with one hand to a chair in a corner which the businessman was to sit on, and he did indeed sit down on it. K. however went very close behind Leni's back, leant over her shoulder and asked, "Who is this man? " Leni put one hand around K. as she stirred the soup with the other, she drew him forward toward herself and said, "He's a pitiful character, a poor businessman by the name of Block. Just look at him. " The two of them looked back over their shoulders. The businessman was sitting on the chair that K. had directed him to, he had extinguished the candle whose light was no longer needed and pressed on the wick with his fingers to stop the smoke. "You were in your nightshirt," said K., putting his hand on her head and turning it back towards the stove. She was silent. "Is he your lover?" asked K. She was about to take hold of the pot of soup, but K. took both her hands and said, "Answer me!" She said, "Come into the office, I'll explain everything to you." "No," said K., "I want you to explain it here. " She put her arms around him and wanted to kiss him. K., though, pushed her away and said, "I don't want you to kiss me now." "Josef," said Leni, looking at K. imploringly but frankly in the eyes, "you're not going to be jealous of Mr. Block now, are you? Rudi," she then said, turning to the businessman, "help me out will you, I'm being suspected of something, you can see that, leave the candle alone. " It had looked as though Mr. Block had not been paying attention but he had been following closely. "I don't even know why you might be jealous," he said ingenuously. " Nor do I, actually," said K., looking at the businessman with a smile. Leni laughed out loud and while K. was not paying attention took the opportunity of embracing him and whispering, "Leave him alone, now, you can see what sort of person he is. I've been helping him a little bit because he's an important client of the lawyer's, and no other reason. And what about you? Do you want to speak to the lawyer at this time of day? He's very unwell today, but if you want I'll tell him you're here. But you can certainly spend the night with me. It's so long since you were last here, even the lawyer has been asking about you. Don't neglect your case! And I've got some things to tell you that I've learned about. But now, before anything else, take your coat off!" She helped him off with his coat, took the hat off his head, ran with the things into the hallway to hang them up, then she ran back and saw to the soup. "Do you want me to tell him you're here straight away or take him his soup first?" "Tell him I'm here first," said K. He was in a bad mood, he had originally intended a detailed discussion of his business with Leni, especially the question of his giving the lawyer notice, but now he no longer wanted to because of the presence of the businessman. Now he considered his affair too important to let this little businessman take part in it and perhaps change some of his decisions, and so he called Leni back even though she was already on her way to the lawyer. "Bring him his soup first," he said, "I want him to get his strength up for the discussion with me, he'll need it." "You're a client of the lawyer's too, aren't you," said the businessman quietly from his corner as if he were trying to find this out. It was not, however, taken well. "What business is that of yours?" said K., and Leni said, "Will you be quiet. - I'll take him his soup first then, shall I? " And she poured the soup into a dish. " The only worry then is that he might go to sleep soon after he's eaten." "What I've got to say to him will keep him awake," said K., who still wanted to intimate that he intended some important negotiations with the lawyer, he wanted Leni to ask him what it was and only then to ask her advice. But instead, she just promptly carried out the order he had given her. When she went over to him with the dish she deliberately brushed against him and whispered, "I'll tell him you're here as soon as he's eaten the soup so that I can get you back as soon as possible." "Just go," said K., "just go." "Be a bit more friendly," she said and, still holding the dish, turned completely round once more in the doorway.

translation: The first ring at the lawyer’s door, as usual, was useless. "Leni could be more spry," thought K. But it was a benefit that the other party did not intervene, as they normally did, whether it was the man in the dressing gown or someone else who started pestering. As K. pressed the bell for the second time, he glanced back at the other door, which remained closed as before. Finally, two eyes appeared at the peephole of the lawyer’s door, though they were not Leni’s eyes. Someone opened the door but held it ajar for a while, shouted back into the apartment: "It’s him!" and only fully opened it after that. K. had pushed against the door, for he already heard the key being hastily turned in the lock of the other apartment door behind him. When the door finally opened before him, he rushed straight into the anteroom and saw, through the corridor leading between the rooms, Leni, to whom the warning shout of the door opener had applied, dashing off in his shirt. He watched her for a while and then looked around for the door opener. He was a small, gaunt man with a full beard, holding a candle in his hand. "You are employed here?" K. asked. "No," the man replied, "I am a stranger here, the lawyer is only my representative; I am here on a legal matter." "Without a coat?" K. asked, gesturing with his hand at the man’s inadequate attire. "Oh, pardon me!" the man said and lit himself with the candle as if seeing his state for the first time. "Is she your lover?" K. asked bluntly. He had spread his legs slightly and held his hat in his hands behind his back. Feeling superior through the mere possession of a great overcoat, he regarded the thin man as inferior. "Oh God," said the man and raised one hand in shocked rejection to his face, "no, no, what do you think?" "You look credible," K. said, smiling, "even so—come in." He waved his hat and let the man precede him. "What’s your name?" K. asked on the way. "Block, businessman Block," the man replied and turned around when making this statement, but K. did not let him stop. "Is that your real name?" K. asked. "Certainly," was the answer, "why do you doubt it?" "I thought you might have a reason to hide your name," said K. He felt so free as one does in talking to lowly people in a foreign land, keeping all that concerns himself to himself and calmly talking about the interests of others, thereby elevating them while having the option of disregarding them at will. At the door to the lawyer’s office, K. stopped, opened it, and shouted to the businessman, who had obediently continued walking: "Not so quickly! Shine a light here!" K. thought Leni might be hiding here, so he made the businessman search every corner, but the room was empty. Before the painting of the judge, K. held the businessman back by the waistband of his trousers. "Do you know him?" he asked and pointed with his index finger up. The businessman raised the candle, blinked, and said: "He’s a judge." "A high judge?" K. asked and stepped to one side of the businessman to observe the impression the picture made on him. The businessman looked up in awe. "He’s a high judge," he said. "You don’t have much insight," said K. "Among the low inquisitor judges, he’s the lowest." "Now I remember," said the businessman and lowered the candle, "I’ve heard it, too." "But of course," K. exclaimed, "I forgot, of course you’ve heard it, too." "But why, why, why," asked the businessman, while he was being pushed towards the door by K.’s hands. Outside the corridor, K. said: "Do you know where Leni is hiding?" "Hiding? " said the businessman, "no, she must be in the kitchen and cooking soup for the lawyer." "Why didn’t you say so before?" K. asked. "I wanted to take you there, but you called me back," the businessman replied, bewildered by the contradictory orders. "Do you think you’re very clever?" K. said. "Lead me then!" On the kitchen, K. had never been, and it was surprisingly large and well-equipped. The stove alone was three times the size of a regular stove, and one couldn’t see the rest of the kitchen details because it was now lit only by a small lamp hanging at the entrance. Leni, in her white apron as always, was standing at the stove, stirring eggs into a pot on a spirit fire. "Evening, Josef," she said with a sideways glance. "Evening," said K. and gestured with a hand to a chair to the side, which the businessman sat on. But K. went close behind Leni, leaned over her shoulder, and asked: "Who is the man?" Leni took K. by the hand, the other stirring the soup, pulled him forward, and said: "He’s a pitiful person, a poor businessman, a certain Block. Look at him." Both turned around. The businessman sat on the chair K. had indicated, had blown out the candle, whose light was no longer needed, and pressed his fingers to the wick to avoid smoke. "You were in your shirt," said K. and turned her head with his hand back to the stove. She was silent. "Is he your lover?" K. asked. She wanted to reach for the soup pot, but K. took her both hands and said: "Now answer!" She said: "Come to the office, I’ll explain everything to you." "No," said K., "I want you to explain it here." She clung to him and wanted to kiss him. K. repelled her and said: "I don’t want you to kiss me now." "Josef," said Leni and looked at K. pleadingly, yet with a candid gaze, "you won’t be jealous of Mr. Block, will you? – Rudi," she said then, turning to the businessman, "help me, you see, I’m being suspected, put the candle down." One might have thought he hadn’t paid attention, but he was completely in the know. "I wouldn’t know why you should be jealous," he said in a somewhat blunt manner. "I don’t really know, either," said K. and looked at the businessman with a smile. Leni laughed loudly, used K.’s inattention to wrap her arms around his, and whispered: "Let him be, you see who he is. I’ve taken a liking to him because he’s a large client of the lawyer, for no other reason. And you? Do you still want to see the lawyer today? He’s very ill today, but if you do, I’ll take you on. But you have to stay here with me tonight, for sure. You haven’t been here for so long, even the lawyer has inquired about you. Don’t neglect the case! I have a few things to tell you, things I’ve found out. Now then, take off your coat first!" She helped him undress, took his hat off, ran with the things to the anteroom, hung them up, and then checked the soup. "Should I bring him the soup first or register you first?" "Register me first," said the businessman softly from his corner. This was not well received. "What does that matter to you?" said K., and Leni said: "Be quiet. – Then I’ll bring him the soup first," said Leni to K. and poured the soup into a bowl. "It’s then to be feared that he’ll fall asleep after the meal, he always falls asleep after eating." "What I have to tell him will keep him awake," said K. He always wanted to make it clear that he had something important to discuss with the lawyer, and he wanted to be asked what it was by Leni and then ask her for advice. But she only fulfilled the explicitly given commands. When she passed by him with the cup, she deliberately nudged him lightly and whispered: "If he’s finished the soup, I’ll register you right away so I can have you back as soon as possible." "Go on then," said K., "go on." "Be kinder," she said and turned around completely in the door with the cup.
source_text: Das erste Läuten an der Tür des Advokaten war, wie gewöhnlich, zwecklos. »Leni könnte flinker sein«, dachte K. Aber es war schon ein Vorteil, wenn sich nicht die andere Partei einmischte, wie sie es gewöhnlich tat, sei es, daß der Mann im Schlafrock oder sonst jemand zu belästigen anfing. Während K. zum zweitenmal den Knopf drückte, sah er nach der anderen Tür zurück, diesmal aber blieb auch sie geschlossen. Endlich erschienen an dem Guckfenster der Tür des Advokaten zwei Augen, es waren aber nicht Lenis Augen. Jemand schloß die Tür auf, stemmte sich aber vorläufig noch gegen sie, rief in die Wohnung zurück: »Er ist es!« und öffnete erst dann vollständig. K. hatte gegen die Tür gedrängt, denn schon hörte er, wie hinter ihm in der Tür der anderen Wohnung der Schlüssel hastig im Schloß gedreht wurde. Als sich daher die Tür vor ihm endlich öffnete, stürmte er geradezu ins Vorzimmer und sah noch, wie durch den Gang, der zwischen den Zimmern hindurchführte, Leni, welcher der Warnungsruf des Türöffners gegolten hatte, im Hemd davonlief. Er blickte ihr ein Weilchen nach und sah sich dann nach dem Türöffner um. Es war ein kleiner, dürrer Mann mit Vollbart, er hielt eine Kerze in der Hand. »Sie sind hier angestellt?« fragte K. »Nein«, antwortete der Mann, »ich bin hier fremd, der Advokat ist nur mein Vertreter, ich bin hier wegen einer Rechtsangelegenheit.« »Ohne Rock?« fragte K. und zeigte mit einer Handbewegung auf die mangelhafte Bekleidung des Mannes. »Ach, verzeihen Sie!« sagte der Mann und beleuchtete sich selbst mit der Kerze, als sähe er selbst zum erstenmal seinen Zustand. »Leni ist Ihre Geliebte?« fragte K. kurz. Er hatte die Beine ein wenig gespreizt, die Hände, in denen er den Hut hielt, hinten verschlungen. Schon durch den Besitz eines starken Überrocks fühlte er sich dem mageren Kleinen sehr überlegen. »O Gott«, sagte der und hob die eine Hand in erschrockener Abwehr vor das Gesicht, »nein, nein, was denken Sie denn?« »Sie sehen glaubwürdig aus«, sagte K. lächelnd, »trotzdem – kommen Sie.« Er winkte ihm mit dem Hut und ließ ihn vor sich gehen. »Wie heißen Sie denn?« fragte K. auf dem Weg. »Block, Kaufmann Block«, sagte der Kleine und drehte sich bei dieser Vorstellung nach K. um, stehenbleiben ließ ihn aber K. nicht. »Ist das Ihr wirklicher Name?« fragte K. »Gewiß«, war die Antwort, »warum haben Sie denn Zweifel?« »Ich dachte, Sie könnten Grund haben, Ihren Namen zu verschweigen«, sagte K. Er fühlte sich so frei, wie man es sonst nur ist, wenn man in der Fremde mit niedrigen Leuten spricht, alles, was einen selbst betrifft, bei sich behält, nur gleichmütig von den Interessen der anderen redet, sie dadurch vor sich selbst erhöht, aber auch nach Belieben fallen lassen kann. Bei der Tür des Arbeitszimmers des Advokaten blieb K. stehen, öffnete sie und rief dem Kaufmann, der folgsam weitergegangen war, zu: »Nicht so eilig! Leuchten Sie hier!« K. dachte, Leni könnte sich hier versteckt haben, er ließ den Kaufmann alle Winkel absuchen, aber das Zimmer war leer. Vor dem Bild des Richters hielt K. den Kaufmann hinten an den Hosenträgern zurück. »Kennen Sie den?« fragte er und zeigte mit dem Zeigefinger in die Höhe. Der Kaufmann hob die Kerze, sah blinzelnd hinauf und sagte: »Es ist ein Richter.« »Ein hoher Richter?« fragte K. und stellte sich seitlich vor den Kaufmann, um den Eindruck, den das Bild auf ihn machte, zu beobachten. Der Kaufmann sah bewundernd aufwärts. »Es ist ein hoher Richter«, sagte er. »Sie haben keinen großen Einblick«, sagte K. »Unter den niedrigen Untersuchungsrichtern ist er der niedrigste.« »Nun erinnere ich mich«, sagte der Kaufmann und senkte die Kerze, »ich habe es auch schon gehört.« »Aber natürlich«, rief K., »ich vergaß ja, natürlich müssen Sie es schon gehört haben.« »Aber warum denn, warum denn«? fragte der Kaufmann, während er sich, von K. mit den Händen angetrieben, zur Tür fortbewegte. Draußen auf dem Gang sagte K.: »Sie wissen doch, wo sich Leni versteckt hat?« »Versteckt?« sagte der Kaufmann, »nein, sie dürfte aber in der Küche sein und dem Advokaten eine Suppe kochen.« »Warum haben Sie das nicht gleich gesagt?« fragte K. »Ich wollte Sie ja hinführen, Sie haben mich aber wieder zurückgerufen«, antwortete der Kaufmann, wie verwirrt durch die widersprechenden Befehle. »Sie glauben wohl sehr schlau zu sein«, sagte K., »führen Sie mich also!« In der Küche war K. noch nie gewesen, sie war überraschend groß und reich ausgestattet. Allein der Herd war dreimal so groß wie gewöhnliche Herde, von dem übrigen sah man keine Einzelheiten, denn die Küche wurde jetzt nur von einer kleinen Lampe beleuchtet, die beim Eingang hing. Am Herd stand Leni in weißer Schürze, wie immer, und leerte Eier in einen Topf aus, der auf einem Spiritusfeuer stand. »Guten Abend, Josef«, sagte sie mit einem Seitenblick. »Guten Abend«, sagte K. und zeigte mit einer Hand auf einen abseits stehenden Sessel, auf den sich der Kaufmann setzen sollte, was dieser auch tat. K. aber ging ganz nahe hinter Leni, beugte sich über ihre Schulter und fragte: »Wer ist der Mann?« Leni umfaßte K. mit einer Hand, die andere quirlte die Suppe, zog ihn nach vorn zu sich und sagte: »Es ist ein bedauernswerter Mensch, ein armer Kaufmann, ein gewisser Block. Sieh ihn nur an.« Sie blickten beide zurück. Der Kaufmann saß auf dem Sessel, auf den ihn K. gewiesen hatte, er hatte die Kerze, deren Licht jetzt unnötig war, ausgepustet und drückte mit den Fingern den Docht, um den Rauch zu verhindern. »Du warst im Hemd«, sagte K. und wendete ihren Kopf mit der Hand wieder dem Herd zu. Sie schwieg. »Er ist dein Geliebter?« fragte K. Sie wollte nach dem Suppentopf greifen, aber K. nahm ihre beiden Hände und sagte: »Nun antworte!« Sie sagte: »Komm ins Arbeitszimmer, ich werde dir alles erklären.« »Nein«, sagte K., »ich will, daß du es hier erklärst.« Sie hing sich an ihn und wollte ihn küssen. K. wehrte sie aber ab und sagte: »Ich will nicht, daß du mich jetzt küßt.« »Josef«, sagte Leni und sah K. bittend und doch offen in die Augen, »du wirst doch nicht auf Herrn Block eifersüchtig sein. – Rudi«, sagte sie dann, sich an den Kaufmann wendend, »so hilf mir doch, du siehst, ich werde verdächtigt, laß die Kerze.« Man hätte denken können, er hätte nicht achtgegeben, aber er war vollständig eingeweiht. »Ich wüßte auch nicht, warum Sie eifersüchtig sein sollten«, sagte er wenig schlagfertig. »Ich weiß es eigentlich auch nicht«, sagte K. und sah den Kaufmann lächelnd an. Leni lachte laut, benützte die Unaufmerksamkeit K.s, um sich in seinen Arm einzuhängen, und flüsterte: »Laß ihn jetzt, du siehst ja, was für ein Mensch er ist. Ich habe mich seiner ein wenig angenommen, weil er eine große Kundschaft des Advokaten ist, aus keinem andern Grund. Und du? Willst du noch heute mit dem Advokaten sprechen? Er ist heute sehr krank, aber wenn du willst, melde ich dich doch an. Über Nacht bleibst du aber bei mir, ganz gewiß. Du warst auch schon so lange nicht bei uns, selbst der Advokat hat nach dir gefragt. Vernachlässige den Prozeß nicht! Auch ich habe dir Verschiedenes mitzuteilen, was ich erfahren habe. Nun aber zieh fürs erste deinen Mantel aus!« Sie half ihm, sich ausziehen, nahm ihm den Hut ab, lief mit den Sachen ins Vorzimmer, sie anzuhängen, lief dann wieder zurück und sah nach der Suppe. »Soll ich zuerst dich anmelden oder ihm zuerst die Suppe bringen?« »Melde mich zuerst an«, sagte K. Er war ärgerlich, er hatte ursprünglich beabsichtigt, mit Leni seine Angelegenheit, insbesondere die fragliche Kündigung genau zu besprechen, die Anwesenheit des Kaufmanns hatte ihm aber die Lust dazu genommen. Jetzt aber hielt er seine Sache doch für zu wichtig, als daß dieser kleine Kaufmann vielleicht entscheidend eingreifen sollte, und so rief er Leni, die schon auf dem Gang war, wieder zurück. »Bring ihm doch zuerst die Suppe«, sagte er, »er soll sich für die Unterredung mit mir stärken, er wird es nötig haben.« »Sie sind auch ein Klient des Advokaten«, sagte, wie zur Feststellung, der Kaufmann leise aus seiner Ecke. Es wurde aber nicht gut aufgenommen. »Was kümmert Sie denn das?« sagte K., und Leni sagte: »Wirst du still sein. – Dann bringe ich ihm also zuerst die Suppe«, sagte Leni zu K. und goß die Suppe auf einen Teller. »Es ist dann nur zu befürchten, daß er bald einschläft, nach dem Essen schläft er bald ein.« »Das, was ich ihm sagen werde, wird ihn wacherhalten«, sagte K., er wollte immerfort durchblicken lassen, daß er etwas Wichtiges mit dem Advokaten zu verhandeln beabsichtige, er wollte von Leni gefragt werden, was es sei, und dann erst sie um Rat fragen. Aber sie erfüllte pünktlich bloß die ausgesprochenen Befehle. Als sie mit der Tasse an ihm vorüberging, stieß sie absichtlich sanft an ihn und flüsterte: »Wenn er die Suppe gegessen hat, melde ich dich gleich an, damit ich dich möglichst bald wiederbekomme.« »Geh nur«, sagte K., »geh nur.« »Sei doch freundlicher«, sagte sie und drehte sich in der Tür mit der Tasse nochmals ganz um.

Now he considered his affair too important to let this little businessman take part in it and perhaps change some of his decisions, and so he called Leni back even though she was already on her way to the lawyer. “Bring him his soup first,” he said, “I want him to get his strength up for the discussion with me, he'll need it.” “You're a client of the lawyer's too, aren't you,” said the businessman quietly from his corner as if he were trying to find this out. human_translations.translator_4: As usual, there was at first no response to K.'s ring at the door. "Leni could be a bit quicker," thought K. But he could at least be glad there was nobody else interfering as usually happened, be it the man in his nightshirt or anyone else who might bother him. As K. pressed on the button for the second time he looked back at the other door, but this time it, too, remained closed. At last, two eyes appeared at the spy-hatch in the lawyer's door, although they weren't Leni's eyes. Someone unlocked the door, but kept himself pressed against it as he called back inside, "It's him!", and only then did he open the door properly. K. pushed against the door, as behind him he could already hear the key being hurriedly turned in the lock of the door to the other flat. When the door in front of him finally opened, he stormed straight into the hallway. Through the corridor which led between the rooms he saw Leni, to whom the warning cry of the door opener had been directed, still running away in her nightshirt. He looked at her for a moment and then looked round at the person who had opened the door. It was a small, wizened man with a full beard, he held a candle in his hand. "Do you work here? " asked K. " No," answered the man, "I don't belong here at all, the lawyer is only representing me, I'm here on legal business." "Without your coat?" asked K., indicating the man's deficiency of dress with a gesture of his hand. "Oh, do forgive me!" said the man, and he looked at himself in the light of the candle he was holding as if he had not known about his appearance until then. "Is Leni your lover? " asked K. curtly. He had set his legs slightly apart, his hands, in which he held his hat, were behind his back. Merely by being in possession of a thick overcoat he felt his advantage over this thin little man. " Oh God," he said and, shocked, raised one hand in front of his face as if in defence, "no, no, what can you be thinking?" "You look honest enough," said K. with a smile, "but come along anyway. " K. indicated with his hat which way the man was to go and let him go ahead of him. "What is your name then?" asked K. on the way. " Block. I'm a businessman," said the small man, twisting himself round as he thus introduced himself, although K. did not allow him to stop moving. "Is that your real name?" asked K. "Of course it is," was the man's reply, "why do you doubt it?" "I thought you might have some reason to keep your name secret," said K. He felt himself as much at liberty as is normally only felt in foreign parts when speaking with people of lower standing, keeping everything about himself to himself, speaking only casually about the interests of the other, able to raise him to a level above one's own, but also able, at will, to let him drop again. K. stopped at the door of the lawyer's office, opened it and, to the businessman who had obediently gone ahead, called, "Not so fast! Bring some light here!" K. thought Leni might have hidden in here, he let the businessman search in every corner, but the room was empty. In front of the picture of the judge K. took hold of the businessman's braces to stop him moving on. " Do you know him?" he asked, pointing upwards with his finger. The businessman lifted the candle, blinked as he looked up and said, "It's a judge." "An important judge?" asked K., and stood to the side and in front of the businessman so that he could observe what impression the picture had on him. The businessman was looking up in admiration. " He's an important judge." "You don't have much insight," said K. " He is the lowest of the lowest examining judges." "I remember now," said the businessman as he lowered the candle, "that's what I've already been told." "Well of course you have," called out K., "I'd forgotten about it, of course you would already have been told." "But why, why?" asked the businessman as he moved forwards towards the door, propelled by the hands of K. Outside in the corridor K. said, "You know where Leni's hidden, do you?" "Hidden?" said the businessman, "No, but she might be in the kitchen cooking soup for the lawyer." "Why didn't you say that immediately?" asked K. "I was going to take you there, but you called me back again," answered the businessman, as if confused by the contradictory commands. "You think you're very clever, don't you," said K, "now take me there!" K. had never been in the kitchen, it was surprisingly big and very well equipped. The stove alone was three times bigger than normal stoves, but it was not possible to see any detail beyond this as the kitchen was at the time illuminated by no more than a small lamp hanging by the entrance. At the stove stood Leni, in a white apron as always, breaking eggs into a pot standing on a spirit lamp. " Good evening, Josef," she said with a glance sideways. " Good evening," said K., pointing with one hand to a chair in a corner which the businessman was to sit on, and he did indeed sit down on it. K. however went very close behind Leni's back, leant over her shoulder and asked, "Who is this man? " Leni put one hand around K. as she stirred the soup with the other, she drew him forward toward herself and said, "He's a pitiful character, a poor businessman by the name of Block. Just look at him. " The two of them looked back over their shoulders. The businessman was sitting on the chair that K. had directed him to, he had extinguished the candle whose light was no longer needed and pressed on the wick with his fingers to stop the smoke. "You were in your nightshirt," said K., putting his hand on her head and turning it back towards the stove. She was silent. "Is he your lover?" asked K. She was about to take hold of the pot of soup, but K. took both her hands and said, "Answer me!" She said, "Come into the office, I'll explain everything to you." "No," said K., "I want you to explain it here. " She put her arms around him and wanted to kiss him. K., though, pushed her away and said, "I don't want you to kiss me now." "Josef," said Leni, looking at K. imploringly but frankly in the eyes, "you're not going to be jealous of Mr. Block now, are you? Rudi," she then said, turning to the businessman, "help me out will you, I'm being suspected of something, you can see that, leave the candle alone. " It had looked as though Mr. Block had not been paying attention but he had been following closely. "I don't even know why you might be jealous," he said ingenuously. " Nor do I, actually," said K., looking at the businessman with a smile. Leni laughed out loud and while K. was not paying attention took the opportunity of embracing him and whispering, "Leave him alone, now, you can see what sort of person he is. I've been helping him a little bit because he's an important client of the lawyer's, and no other reason. And what about you? Do you want to speak to the lawyer at this time of day? She helped him off with his coat, took the hat off his head, ran with the things into the hallway to hang them up, then she ran back and saw to the soup. "Do you want me to tell him you're here straight away or take him his soup first?" "Tell him I'm here first," said K. He was in a bad mood, he had originally intended a detailed discussion of his business with Leni, especially the question of his giving the lawyer notice, but now he no longer wanted to because of the presence of the businessman. Now he considered his affair too important to let this little businessman take part in it and perhaps change some of his decisions, and so he called Leni back even though she was already on her way to the lawyer. "Bring him his soup first," he said, "I want him to get his strength up for the discussion with me, he'll need it." "You're a client of the lawyer's too, aren't you," said the businessman quietly from his corner as if he were trying to find this out. It was not, however, taken well. "What business is that of yours?" said K., and Leni said, "Will you be quiet. - I'll take him his soup first then, shall I? " And she poured the soup into a dish. " The only worry then is that he might go to sleep soon after he's eaten." "What I've got to say to him will keep him awake," said K., who still wanted to intimate that he intended some important negotiations with the lawyer, he wanted Leni to ask him what it was and only then to ask her advice. But instead, she just promptly carried out the order he had given her. When she went over to him with the dish she deliberately brushed against him and whispered, "I'll tell him you're here as soon as he's eaten the soup so that I can get you back as soon as possible." "Just go," said K., "just go." "Be a bit more friendly," she said and, still holding the dish, turned completely round once more in the doorway.

translation: The first ringing at the lawyer's door, as usual, was pointless. "Leni could be more agile," thought K. But it was already an advantage if the other side did not interfere, as they usually did, whether the man in the dressing gown or someone else started to hassle him. While K. pressed the doorbell a second time, he looked back at the other door, but it remained closed as well. Finally, two eyes appeared at the peephole of the lawyer's door, but they were not Leni's eyes. Someone opened the door, held it for a moment, shouted back into the apartment: "It's him!" and only then opened it fully. K. had pressed against the door because he could already hear the key being turned hastily in the lock of the other apartment door behind him. When the door finally opened before him, he rushed straight into the antechamber and saw Leni, who had heard the warning shout of the door opener, run off in her nightshirt through the corridor that led between the rooms. K. watched her for a moment and then looked for the door opener. He was a small, thin man with a full beard, holding a candle in his hand. "Are you employed here?" asked K. "No," answered the man, "I'm just a stranger here, the lawyer is only my representative. I'm here for a legal matter." "Without a coat?" asked K., gesturing to the man's inadequate attire. "Oh, forgive me!" said the man and lit himself up with the candle as if he was seeing his own state for the first time. "Is Leni your lover?" asked K. briefly. He had spread his legs slightly and held his hat in his hands, entwining them at the back. Through the possession of a long overcoat, he felt very superior to the thin man. "Oh, God," said the man, raising one hand in terrified defense to his face, "no, no, what are you thinking?" "You look trustworthy," said K. with a smile, "but still – come in." He waved him with his hat and let him go first. "What is your name?" asked K. as they walked. "Block, merchant Block," said the small man and turned around when he thought of his name, but K. did not let him stop. "Is that your real name?" asked K. "Of course," was the answer. "Why do you have doubts?" "I thought you might have a reason to hide your name," said K. He felt as free as one does when speaking with low people in a foreign land, keeping all that concerned himself to himself, talking only calmly about the interests of others, thereby elevating them, but also leaving them at will. At the door to the lawyer's office, K. stopped, opened the door, and shouted to the merchant, who had obediently continued walking: "Not so quickly! Light the way!" K. thought Leni might be hiding here, so he made the merchant search all corners, but the room was empty. Before the judge's portrait, K. held back the merchant by the waistband of his trousers. "Do you know him?" asked he and pointed with his finger upward. The merchant raised the candle, squinted up, and said: "It's a judge." "A high judge?" asked K. and stood to the side of the merchant to observe the impression that the portrait made on him. The merchant looked up with admiration. "It is a high judge," he said. "You do not have much insight," said K. "Under the low examining judges, he is the lowest." "Now I remember," said the merchant and lowered the candle, "I've heard that too." "But of course," cried K., "I forgot, of course, you must have heard about that." "But why, why," asked the merchant, while K. drove him toward the door with his hands. Outside in the hallway, said K.: "Do you know where Leni is hiding?" "Hiding?" said the merchant, "no, she must be in the kitchen and making soup for the lawyer." "Why didn't you say so at once?" asked K. "I wanted to show you, but you kept calling me back," answered the merchant, bewildered by the contradictory commands. "You must think you're very clever," said K., "lead me then!" K. had never been in the kitchen before, and it was surprisingly large and well-equipped. The stove was three times as big as usual, the rest was invisible, for the kitchen was now only dimly lit by a small lamp hanging at the entrance. Leni stood at the stove in her white apron, as always, emptying eggs into a pot on a spirit stove. "Good evening, Josef," she said with a sideways glance. "Good evening," said K. and gestured with his hand to a chair at the side, where the merchant was to sit, which he did. K. walked up very close behind Leni, leaned over her shoulder, and asked: "Who is that man?" Leni grasped K. with one hand, the other stirred the soup, pulled him forward, and said: "He's a wretched person, a poor merchant, a certain Block. Look at him." They both turned to look. The merchant sat in the chair K. had indicated, he had extinguished the candle whose light was now unnecessary and pressed the wick with his fingers to prevent the smoke. "You were in your shirt," said K. and turned her head to the stove with his hand. She was silent. "Is he your lover?" asked K. She wanted to reach for the soup pot, but K. took both her hands and said: "Now answer!" She said: "Come to the office, I'll explain everything to you." "No," said K., "I want you to explain it here." She clung to him and wanted to kiss him. K. pushed her away and said: "I don't want you to kiss me now." "Josef," said Leni and looked at K. pleadingly and yet open-eyed, "you won't be jealous of Mr. Block, will you? – Rudi," she said then, turning to the merchant, "help me now, you see, I'm being suspected, let go of the candle." One might think he did not pay attention, but he was fully informed. "I wouldn't know why you should be jealous," he said, somewhat inarticulately. "I don't really know either," said K. and looked at the merchant with a smile. Leni laughed loudly, used K.'s inattention to lean into his arms, and whispered: "Leave him now, you see what kind of person he is. I've taken a liking to him because he has a large client base for the lawyer, for no other reason. And you? Do you still want to speak with the lawyer today? He is very ill today, but if you want, I'll arrange it for you. But you'll stay with me tonight, for sure. You haven't been with us for so long, even the lawyer has been asking about you. Don't neglect your case! I have something to tell you as well, something I've learned. Now then, take off your coat first!" She helped him take off his coat, took his hat off, ran with the clothes into the antechamber, then came back and looked at the soup. "Should I first ring you in or bring him the soup first?" "Ring me in first," said K. He was annoyed; he had originally intended to discuss his business with Leni, especially the pending dismissal, but the presence of the merchant had taken away his desire to do so. Now, however, he considered his matter too important for the little merchant to intervene decisively, and so he called Leni back, who was already in the hallway. "Bring him the soup first," he said, "let him have something to strengthen himself for our talk, he will need it." "You are also a client of the lawyer," said the merchant softly from his corner, as if stating a fact. It was not well received. "What does it matter to you?" said K., and Leni said: "Be quiet." – "Then bring him the soup first," said Leni to K. and poured the soup into a bowl. "It can only be feared that he will fall asleep after eating, he often falls asleep after eating." "What I will tell him will keep him awake," said K. He always tried to make it clear that he had something important to discuss with the lawyer and wanted Leni to ask what it was and then ask for his advice. But she only fulfilled the commands given. When she passed with the cup in front of him, she accidentally nudged him gently and whispered: "When he has finished the soup, I will ring you in immediately so that I can get you back as soon as possible." "Go ahead," said K., "go ahead." "Be nicer," she said and turned around with the cup in the door, still completely around.
source_text: Das erste Läuten an der Tür des Advokaten war, wie gewöhnlich, zwecklos. »Leni könnte flinker sein«, dachte K. Aber es war schon ein Vorteil, wenn sich nicht die andere Partei einmischte, wie sie es gewöhnlich tat, sei es, daß der Mann im Schlafrock oder sonst jemand zu belästigen anfing. Während K. zum zweitenmal den Knopf drückte, sah er nach der anderen Tür zurück, diesmal aber blieb auch sie geschlossen. Endlich erschienen an dem Guckfenster der Tür des Advokaten zwei Augen, es waren aber nicht Lenis Augen. Jemand schloß die Tür auf, stemmte sich aber vorläufig noch gegen sie, rief in die Wohnung zurück: »Er ist es!« und öffnete erst dann vollständig. K. hatte gegen die Tür gedrängt, denn schon hörte er, wie hinter ihm in der Tür der anderen Wohnung der Schlüssel hastig im Schloß gedreht wurde. Als sich daher die Tür vor ihm endlich öffnete, stürmte er geradezu ins Vorzimmer und sah noch, wie durch den Gang, der zwischen den Zimmern hindurchführte, Leni, welcher der Warnungsruf des Türöffners gegolten hatte, im Hemd davonlief. Er blickte ihr ein Weilchen nach und sah sich dann nach dem Türöffner um. Es war ein kleiner, dürrer Mann mit Vollbart, er hielt eine Kerze in der Hand. »Sie sind hier angestellt?« fragte K. »Nein«, antwortete der Mann, »ich bin hier fremd, der Advokat ist nur mein Vertreter, ich bin hier wegen einer Rechtsangelegenheit.« »Ohne Rock?« fragte K. und zeigte mit einer Handbewegung auf die mangelhafte Bekleidung des Mannes. »Ach, verzeihen Sie!« sagte der Mann und beleuchtete sich selbst mit der Kerze, als sähe er selbst zum erstenmal seinen Zustand. »Leni ist Ihre Geliebte?« fragte K. kurz. Er hatte die Beine ein wenig gespreizt, die Hände, in denen er den Hut hielt, hinten verschlungen. Schon durch den Besitz eines starken Überrocks fühlte er sich dem mageren Kleinen sehr überlegen. »O Gott«, sagte der und hob die eine Hand in erschrockener Abwehr vor das Gesicht, »nein, nein, was denken Sie denn?« »Sie sehen glaubwürdig aus«, sagte K. lächelnd, »trotzdem – kommen Sie.« Er winkte ihm mit dem Hut und ließ ihn vor sich gehen. »Wie heißen Sie denn?« fragte K. auf dem Weg. »Block, Kaufmann Block«, sagte der Kleine und drehte sich bei dieser Vorstellung nach K. um, stehenbleiben ließ ihn aber K. nicht. »Ist das Ihr wirklicher Name?« fragte K. »Gewiß«, war die Antwort, »warum haben Sie denn Zweifel?« »Ich dachte, Sie könnten Grund haben, Ihren Namen zu verschweigen«, sagte K. Er fühlte sich so frei, wie man es sonst nur ist, wenn man in der Fremde mit niedrigen Leuten spricht, alles, was einen selbst betrifft, bei sich behält, nur gleichmütig von den Interessen der anderen redet, sie dadurch vor sich selbst erhöht, aber auch nach Belieben fallen lassen kann. Bei der Tür des Arbeitszimmers des Advokaten blieb K. stehen, öffnete sie und rief dem Kaufmann, der folgsam weitergegangen war, zu: »Nicht so eilig! Leuchten Sie hier!« K. dachte, Leni könnte sich hier versteckt haben, er ließ den Kaufmann alle Winkel absuchen, aber das Zimmer war leer. Vor dem Bild des Richters hielt K. den Kaufmann hinten an den Hosenträgern zurück. »Kennen Sie den?« fragte er und zeigte mit dem Zeigefinger in die Höhe. Der Kaufmann hob die Kerze, sah blinzelnd hinauf und sagte: »Es ist ein Richter.« »Ein hoher Richter?« fragte K. und stellte sich seitlich vor den Kaufmann, um den Eindruck, den das Bild auf ihn machte, zu beobachten. Der Kaufmann sah bewundernd aufwärts. »Es ist ein hoher Richter«, sagte er. »Sie haben keinen großen Einblick«, sagte K. »Unter den niedrigen Untersuchungsrichtern ist er der niedrigste.« »Nun erinnere ich mich«, sagte der Kaufmann und senkte die Kerze, »ich habe es auch schon gehört.« »Aber natürlich«, rief K., »ich vergaß ja, natürlich müssen Sie es schon gehört haben.« »Aber warum denn, warum denn«? fragte der Kaufmann, während er sich, von K. mit den Händen angetrieben, zur Tür fortbewegte. Draußen auf dem Gang sagte K.: »Sie wissen doch, wo sich Leni versteckt hat?« »Versteckt?« sagte der Kaufmann, »nein, sie dürfte aber in der Küche sein und dem Advokaten eine Suppe kochen.« »Warum haben Sie das nicht gleich gesagt?« fragte K. »Ich wollte Sie ja hinführen, Sie haben mich aber wieder zurückgerufen«, antwortete der Kaufmann, wie verwirrt durch die widersprechenden Befehle. »Sie glauben wohl sehr schlau zu sein«, sagte K., »führen Sie mich also!« In der Küche war K. noch nie gewesen, sie war überraschend groß und reich ausgestattet. Allein der Herd war dreimal so groß wie gewöhnliche Herde, von dem übrigen sah man keine Einzelheiten, denn die Küche wurde jetzt nur von einer kleinen Lampe beleuchtet, die beim Eingang hing. Am Herd stand Leni in weißer Schürze, wie immer, und leerte Eier in einen Topf aus, der auf einem Spiritusfeuer stand. »Guten Abend, Josef«, sagte sie mit einem Seitenblick. »Guten Abend«, sagte K. und zeigte mit einer Hand auf einen abseits stehenden Sessel, auf den sich der Kaufmann setzen sollte, was dieser auch tat. K. aber ging ganz nahe hinter Leni, beugte sich über ihre Schulter und fragte: »Wer ist der Mann?« Leni umfaßte K. mit einer Hand, die andere quirlte die Suppe, zog ihn nach vorn zu sich und sagte: »Es ist ein bedauernswerter Mensch, ein armer Kaufmann, ein gewisser Block. Sieh ihn nur an.« Sie blickten beide zurück. Der Kaufmann saß auf dem Sessel, auf den ihn K. gewiesen hatte, er hatte die Kerze, deren Licht jetzt unnötig war, ausgepustet und drückte mit den Fingern den Docht, um den Rauch zu verhindern. »Du warst im Hemd«, sagte K. und wendete ihren Kopf mit der Hand wieder dem Herd zu. Sie schwieg. »Er ist dein Geliebter?« fragte K. Sie wollte nach dem Suppentopf greifen, aber K. nahm ihre beiden Hände und sagte: »Nun antworte!« Sie sagte: »Komm ins Arbeitszimmer, ich werde dir alles erklären.« »Nein«, sagte K., »ich will, daß du es hier erklärst.« Sie hing sich an ihn und wollte ihn küssen. K. wehrte sie aber ab und sagte: »Ich will nicht, daß du mich jetzt küßt.« »Josef«, sagte Leni und sah K. bittend und doch offen in die Augen, »du wirst doch nicht auf Herrn Block eifersüchtig sein. – Rudi«, sagte sie dann, sich an den Kaufmann wendend, »so hilf mir doch, du siehst, ich werde verdächtigt, laß die Kerze.« Man hätte denken können, er hätte nicht achtgegeben, aber er war vollständig eingeweiht. »Ich wüßte auch nicht, warum Sie eifersüchtig sein sollten«, sagte er wenig schlagfertig. »Ich weiß es eigentlich auch nicht«, sagte K. und sah den Kaufmann lächelnd an. Leni lachte laut, benützte die Unaufmerksamkeit K.s, um sich in seinen Arm einzuhängen, und flüsterte: »Laß ihn jetzt, du siehst ja, was für ein Mensch er ist. Ich habe mich seiner ein wenig angenommen, weil er eine große Kundschaft des Advokaten ist, aus keinem andern Grund. Und du? Willst du noch heute mit dem Advokaten sprechen? Er ist heute sehr krank, aber wenn du willst, melde ich dich doch an. Über Nacht bleibst du aber bei mir, ganz gewiß. Du warst auch schon so lange nicht bei uns, selbst der Advokat hat nach dir gefragt. Vernachlässige den Prozeß nicht! Auch ich habe dir Verschiedenes mitzuteilen, was ich erfahren habe. Nun aber zieh fürs erste deinen Mantel aus!« Sie half ihm, sich ausziehen, nahm ihm den Hut ab, lief mit den Sachen ins Vorzimmer, sie anzuhängen, lief dann wieder zurück und sah nach der Suppe. »Soll ich zuerst dich anmelden oder ihm zuerst die Suppe bringen?« »Melde mich zuerst an«, sagte K. Er war ärgerlich, er hatte ursprünglich beabsichtigt, mit Leni seine Angelegenheit, insbesondere die fragliche Kündigung genau zu besprechen, die Anwesenheit des Kaufmanns hatte ihm aber die Lust dazu genommen. Jetzt aber hielt er seine Sache doch für zu wichtig, als daß dieser kleine Kaufmann vielleicht entscheidend eingreifen sollte, und so rief er Leni, die schon auf dem Gang war, wieder zurück. »Bring ihm doch zuerst die Suppe«, sagte er, »er soll sich für die Unterredung mit mir stärken, er wird es nötig haben.« »Sie sind auch ein Klient des Advokaten«, sagte, wie zur Feststellung, der Kaufmann leise aus seiner Ecke. Es wurde aber nicht gut aufgenommen. »Was kümmert Sie denn das?« sagte K., und Leni sagte: »Wirst du still sein. – Dann bringe ich ihm also zuerst die Suppe«, sagte Leni zu K. und goß die Suppe auf einen Teller. »Es ist dann nur zu befürchten, daß er bald einschläft, nach dem Essen schläft er bald ein.« »Das, was ich ihm sagen werde, wird ihn wacherhalten«, sagte K., er wollte immerfort durchblicken lassen, daß er etwas Wichtiges mit dem Advokaten zu verhandeln beabsichtige, er wollte von Leni gefragt werden, was es sei, und dann erst sie um Rat fragen. Aber sie erfüllte pünktlich bloß die ausgesprochenen Befehle. Als sie mit der Tasse an ihm vorüberging, stieß sie absichtlich sanft an ihn und flüsterte: »Wenn er die Suppe gegessen hat, melde ich dich gleich an, damit ich dich möglichst bald wiederbekomme.« »Geh nur«, sagte K., »geh nur.« »Sei doch freundlicher«, sagte sie und drehte sich in der Tür mit der Tasse nochmals ganz um.

Now he considered his affair too important to let this little businessman take part in it and perhaps change some of his decisions, and so he called Leni back even though she was already on her way to the lawyer. “Bring him his soup first,” he said, “I want him to get his strength up for the discussion with me, he'll need it.” “You're a client of the lawyer's too, aren't you,” said the businessman quietly from his corner as if he were trying to find this out. It was not, however, taken well. “What business is that of yours?” said K., and Leni said, “Will you be quiet.—I'll take him his soup first then, shall I?” And she poured the soup into a dish. “The only worry then is that he might go to sleep soon after he's eaten.” “What I've got to say to him will keep him awake,” said K., who still wanted to intimate that he intended some important negotiations with the lawyer, he wanted Leni to ask him what it was and only then to ask her advice. But instead, she just promptly carried out the order he had given her. When she went over to him with the dish she deliberately brushed against him and whispered, “I'll tell him you're here as soon as he's eaten the soup so that I can get you back as soon as possible.” “Just go,” said K., “just go.” “Be a bit more friendly,” she said and, still holding the dish, turned completely round once more in the doorway.
human_translations.translator_4: As usual, there was at first no response to K.'s ring at the door. "Leni could be a bit quicker," thought K. But he could at least be glad there was nobody else interfering as usually happened, be it the man in his nightshirt or anyone else who might bother him. As K. pressed on the button for the second time he looked back at the other door, but this time it, too, remained closed. At last, two eyes appeared at the spy-hatch in the lawyer's door, although they weren't Leni's eyes. Someone unlocked the door, but kept himself pressed against it as he called back inside, "It's him!", and only then did he open the door properly. K. pushed against the door, as behind him he could already hear the key being hurriedly turned in the lock of the door to the other flat. When the door in front of him finally opened, he stormed straight into the hallway. Through the corridor which led between the rooms he saw Leni, to whom the warning cry of the door opener had been directed, still running away in her nightshirt. He looked at her for a moment and then looked round at the person who had opened the door. It was a small, wizened man with a full beard, he held a candle in his hand. "Do you work here? " asked K. " No," answered the man, "I don't belong here at all, the lawyer is only representing me, I'm here on legal business." "Without your coat?" asked K., indicating the man's deficiency of dress with a gesture of his hand. "Oh, do forgive me!" said the man, and he looked at himself in the light of the candle he was holding as if he had not known about his appearance until then. "Is Leni your lover? " asked K. curtly. He had set his legs slightly apart, his hands, in which he held his hat, were behind his back. Merely by being in possession of a thick overcoat he felt his advantage over this thin little man. " Oh God," he said and, shocked, raised one hand in front of his face as if in defence, "no, no, what can you be thinking?" "You look honest enough," said K. with a smile, "but come along anyway. " K. indicated with his hat which way the man was to go and let him go ahead of him. "What is your name then?" asked K. on the way. " Block. I'm a businessman," said the small man, twisting himself round as he thus introduced himself, although K. did not allow him to stop moving. "Is that your real name?" asked K. "Of course it is," was the man's reply, "why do you doubt it?" "I thought you might have some reason to keep your name secret," said K. He felt himself as much at liberty as is normally only felt in foreign parts when speaking with people of lower standing, keeping everything about himself to himself, speaking only casually about the interests of the other, able to raise him to a level above one's own, but also able, at will, to let him drop again. K. stopped at the door of the lawyer's office, opened it and, to the businessman who had obediently gone ahead, called, "Not so fast! Bring some light here!" K. thought Leni might have hidden in here, he let the businessman search in every corner, but the room was empty. In front of the picture of the judge K. took hold of the businessman's braces to stop him moving on. " Do you know him?" he asked, pointing upwards with his finger. The businessman lifted the candle, blinked as he looked up and said, "It's a judge." "An important judge?" asked K., and stood to the side and in front of the businessman so that he could observe what impression the picture had on him. The businessman was looking up in admiration. " He's an important judge." "You don't have much insight," said K. " He is the lowest of the lowest examining judges." "I remember now," said the businessman as he lowered the candle, "that's what I've already been told." "Well of course you have," called out K., "I'd forgotten about it, of course you would already have been told." "But why, why?" asked the businessman as he moved forwards towards the door, propelled by the hands of K. Outside in the corridor K. said, "You know where Leni's hidden, do you?" "Hidden?" said the businessman, "No, but she might be in the kitchen cooking soup for the lawyer." "Why didn't you say that immediately?" asked K. "I was going to take you there, but you called me back again," answered the businessman, as if confused by the contradictory commands. "You think you're very clever, don't you," said K, "now take me there!" K. had never been in the kitchen, it was surprisingly big and very well equipped. The stove alone was three times bigger than normal stoves, but it was not possible to see any detail beyond this as the kitchen was at the time illuminated by no more than a small lamp hanging by the entrance. At the stove stood Leni, in a white apron as always, breaking eggs into a pot standing on a spirit lamp. " Good evening, Josef," she said with a glance sideways. " Good evening," said K., pointing with one hand to a chair in a corner which the businessman was to sit on, and he did indeed sit down on it. K. however went very close behind Leni's back, leant over her shoulder and asked, "Who is this man? " Leni put one hand around K. as she stirred the soup with the other, she drew him forward toward herself and said, "He's a pitiful character, a poor businessman by the name of Block. Just look at him. " The two of them looked back over their shoulders. The businessman was sitting on the chair that K. had directed him to, he had extinguished the candle whose light was no longer needed and pressed on the wick with his fingers to stop the smoke. "You were in your nightshirt," said K., putting his hand on her head and turning it back towards the stove. She was silent. "Is he your lover?" asked K. She was about to take hold of the pot of soup, but K. took both her hands and said, "Answer me!" She said, "Come into the office, I'll explain everything to you." "No," said K., "I want you to explain it here. " She put her arms around him and wanted to kiss him. K., though, pushed her away and said, "I don't want you to kiss me now." "Josef," said Leni, looking at K. imploringly but frankly in the eyes, "you're not going to be jealous of Mr. Block now, are you? Rudi," she then said, turning to the businessman, "help me out will you, I'm being suspected of something, you can see that, leave the candle alone. " It had looked as though Mr. Block had not been paying attention but he had been following closely. "I don't even know why you might be jealous," he said ingenuously. " Nor do I, actually," said K., looking at the businessman with a smile. Leni laughed out loud and while K. was not paying attention took the opportunity of embracing him and whispering, "Leave him alone, now, you can see what sort of person he is. I've been helping him a little bit because he's an important client of the lawyer's, and no other reason. And what about you? Do you want to speak to the lawyer at this time of day? He's very unwell today, but if you want I'll tell him you're here. But you can certainly spend the night with me. It's so long since you were last here, even the lawyer has been asking about you. Don't neglect your case! And I've got some things to tell you that I've learned about. But now, before anything else, take your coat off!" She helped him off with his coat, took the hat off his head, ran with the things into the hallway to hang them up, then she ran back and saw to the soup. "Do you want me to tell him you're here straight away or take him his soup first?" "Tell him I'm here first," said K. He was in a bad mood, he had originally intended a detailed discussion of his business with Leni, especially the question of his giving the lawyer notice, but now he no longer wanted to because of the presence of the businessman. Now he considered his affair too important to let this little businessman take part in it and perhaps change some of his decisions, and so he called Leni back even though she was already on her way to the lawyer. "Bring him his soup first," he said, "I want him to get his strength up for the discussion with me, he'll need it." "You're a client of the lawyer's too, aren't you," said the businessman quietly from his corner as if he were trying to find this out. It was not, however, taken well. "What business is that of yours?" said K., and Leni said, "Will you be quiet. - I'll take him his soup first then, shall I? " And she poured the soup into a dish. " The only worry then is that he might go to sleep soon after he's eaten." "What I've got to say to him will keep him awake," said K., who still wanted to intimate that he intended some important negotiations with the lawyer, he wanted Leni to ask him what it was and only then to ask her advice. But instead, she just promptly carried out the order he had given her. When she went over to him with the dish she deliberately brushed against him and whispered, "I'll tell him you're here as soon as he's eaten the soup so that I can get you back as soon as possible." "Just go," said K., "just go." "Be a bit more friendly," she said and, still holding the dish, turned completely round once more in the doorway.

translation: The first ring at the lawyer's door, as usual, was futile. "Leni could be more nimble," K thought. But it was already an advantage that the other party didn't intervene, as was usually the case—whether it was the man in the dressing gown or someone else starting to harass. As K pressed the doorbell for the second time, he looked back at the other door, but that one stayed closed as well. Finally, two eyes appeared at the peephole, though they were not Leni's. Someone opened the door but pressed against it for a moment, shouted back into the apartment, "It's him!" and only fully opened it afterward. K had pushed against the door, for he heard the key being hastily turned in the lock on the other side. When the door finally opened before him, he rushed straight into the anteroom and saw through the hallway that Leni, who had received the warning shout from the door opener, was running away in her shirt. He watched her for a while and then looked for the door opener. He was a small, slender man with a full beard, holding a candle in his hand. "Are you employed here?" K asked. "No," replied the man, "I'm a stranger here; the lawyer is just my representative, I'm here for a legal matter." "Without a coat?" asked K, motioning to the man's incomplete attire. "Ah, forgive me!" said the man and illuminated himself with the candle as if he had just noticed his condition for the first time. "Is Leni your lover?" K asked abruptly. He had spread his legs slightly and held his hat in his hands, intertwined at the back. Already with the possession of a substantial overcoat, he felt very superior to the emaciated little man. "Oh God," said the man, raising one hand in surprised defense to his face, "no, no, what do you think?" "You look credible," said K, smiling, "still, come in." He waved at him with his hat and let him go ahead. "What is your name?" K asked on the way. "Block, trading block," said the small man and turned around to look at K as he spoke, but K did not let him stop. "Is that your real name?" K asked. "Of course," was the reply, "why do you doubt?" "I thought you might have a reason to hide your name," said K. He felt so free as one is only in a foreign place with lowly people, keeping everything that concerned him to himself, only calmly talking about the interests of others, thereby elevating them, but also able to let them fall at any time. At the door of the lawyer's office, K stopped, opened the door, and shouted to the trader, who had obediently continued walking, "Not so rushed! Shine a light here!" K thought Leni might be hiding there, and he made the trader search all the corners, but the room was empty. In front of the judge's portrait, K held back the trader by the waistbands of his trousers. "Do you know him?" he asked, pointing up with his finger. The trader raised the candle, blinked, and said, "It's a judge." "A high judge?" K asked and stepped sideways to the trader to observe the impression the portrait made on him. The trader looked up in admiration. "It's a high judge," he said. "You have no great insight," said K, "among the low investigative judges, he is the lowest." "Now I remember," said the trader and lowered the candle, "I've heard about it." "But of course," K exclaimed, "I forgot, of course, you must have heard about it too." "But why, why," the trader asked, while K, with his hands, urged him toward the door. Outside in the hallway, said K, "Do you know where Leni is hiding?" "Hiding?" said the trader, "no, she should be in the kitchen and cooking a soup for the lawyer." "Why didn't you say that at once?" K asked. "I wanted to lead you there, but you called me back again," answered the trader, bewildered by the contradictory orders. "You must think you're very clever," said K, "lead me then!" K had never been in the kitchen before; it was surprisingly large and richly equipped. The stove alone was three times as big as an ordinary one, and one could not see the rest of the kitchen, as it was now illuminated only by a small lamp hanging at the entrance. By the stove stood Leni in her white apron, as always, emptying eggs into a pot on a spirit stove. "Evening, Josef," she said with a sidelong glance. "Evening," said K, and indicated with his hand a chair by the side, which the trader sat down in. But K went very close behind Leni, bent over her shoulder, and asked, "Who is the man?" Leni grasped K with one hand, while the other stirred the soup, pulled him closer, and said, "He is a pitiful person, a poor trader, a certain Block. Just look at him." Both looked back. The trader sat in the chair K had pointed to, had blown out the candle whose light was now unnecessary, and pressed the wick to prevent smoke. "You were in your shirt," said K and turned her head to the stove with his hand. She remained silent. "Is he your lover?" K asked. She wanted to reach for the soup pot, but K took her hands and said, "Answer now!" She said, "Come into the office, I'll explain everything to you." "No," said K, "I want you to explain it here." She clung to him and wanted to kiss him. K, however, repelled her and said, "I don't want you to kiss me now." "Josef," said Leni and looked at K pleadingly but open in the eyes, "you won't be jealous of Mr. Block, will you? – Rudi," she then said, turning to the trader, "help me, you see, I'm suspected, let go of the candle." One could think he did not pay attention, but he was fully informed. "I wouldn't know why you should be jealous," he said, not very wittily. "I don't know either," said K and looked at the trader with a smile. Leni laughed loudly, used K's inattention to cling to his arm, and whispered, "Let him be, you see what kind of person he is. I took him on a little because he is a large client of the lawyer, for no other reason. And you? Do you still want to talk to the lawyer today? He is very ill today, but if you want, I'll register you anyway. But you will stay with me overnight, for sure. You haven't been with us for such a long time, even the lawyer has asked about you. Don't neglect the case! I have several things to tell you too, what I've learned. Now take off your coat first!" She helped him take off his coat, took off his hat, ran with the things into the anteroom, and then went back to check the soup. "Should I register you first or bring the soup to him first?" "Register me first," said K. He was annoyed; he had originally intended to discuss with Leni his matter, especially the disputed termination, but the presence of the trader had robbed him of his enthusiasm. Now, however, he felt that his matter was too important to be decided by this small trader, and so he called Leni, who was already in the hallway, back. "Bring him the soup first," he said, "let him have the strength to talk with me after eating, he will need it." "You are also a client of the lawyer," said the trader, in a low voice from his corner as a matter of fact. It was not well received. "What does it matter to you?" said K, and Leni said, "Be quiet. – Then I will bring him the soup first," said Leni to K and poured the soup into a plate. "It will only be feared that he will fall asleep after eating, he will probably fall asleep soon." "What I have to say to him will keep him awake," said K, he always wanted to hint that he had something important to discuss with the lawyer and would want to be asked by Leni what it was and then only ask for her advice. But she fulfilled the given orders punctually. When she passed him with the cup, she nudged him gently and whispered, "When he has finished the soup, I'll register you at once so that I can get you back as soon as possible." "Go on then," said K, "go on." "Be kind," she said and turned around in the doorway with the cup.
source_text: Das erste Läuten an der Tür des Advokaten war, wie gewöhnlich, zwecklos. »Leni könnte flinker sein«, dachte K. Aber es war schon ein Vorteil, wenn sich nicht die andere Partei einmischte, wie sie es gewöhnlich tat, sei es, daß der Mann im Schlafrock oder sonst jemand zu belästigen anfing. Während K. zum zweitenmal den Knopf drückte, sah er nach der anderen Tür zurück, diesmal aber blieb auch sie geschlossen. Endlich erschienen an dem Guckfenster der Tür des Advokaten zwei Augen, es waren aber nicht Lenis Augen. Jemand schloß die Tür auf, stemmte sich aber vorläufig noch gegen sie, rief in die Wohnung zurück: »Er ist es!« und öffnete erst dann vollständig. K. hatte gegen die Tür gedrängt, denn schon hörte er, wie hinter ihm in der Tür der anderen Wohnung der Schlüssel hastig im Schloß gedreht wurde. Als sich daher die Tür vor ihm endlich öffnete, stürmte er geradezu ins Vorzimmer und sah noch, wie durch den Gang, der zwischen den Zimmern hindurchführte, Leni, welcher der Warnungsruf des Türöffners gegolten hatte, im Hemd davonlief. Er blickte ihr ein Weilchen nach und sah sich dann nach dem Türöffner um. Es war ein kleiner, dürrer Mann mit Vollbart, er hielt eine Kerze in der Hand. »Sie sind hier angestellt?« fragte K. »Nein«, antwortete der Mann, »ich bin hier fremd, der Advokat ist nur mein Vertreter, ich bin hier wegen einer Rechtsangelegenheit.« »Ohne Rock?« fragte K. und zeigte mit einer Handbewegung auf die mangelhafte Bekleidung des Mannes. »Ach, verzeihen Sie!« sagte der Mann und beleuchtete sich selbst mit der Kerze, als sähe er selbst zum erstenmal seinen Zustand. »Leni ist Ihre Geliebte?« fragte K. kurz. Er hatte die Beine ein wenig gespreizt, die Hände, in denen er den Hut hielt, hinten verschlungen. Schon durch den Besitz eines starken Überrocks fühlte er sich dem mageren Kleinen sehr überlegen. »O Gott«, sagte der und hob die eine Hand in erschrockener Abwehr vor das Gesicht, »nein, nein, was denken Sie denn?« »Sie sehen glaubwürdig aus«, sagte K. lächelnd, »trotzdem – kommen Sie.« Er winkte ihm mit dem Hut und ließ ihn vor sich gehen. »Wie heißen Sie denn?« fragte K. auf dem Weg. »Block, Kaufmann Block«, sagte der Kleine und drehte sich bei dieser Vorstellung nach K. um, stehenbleiben ließ ihn aber K. nicht. »Ist das Ihr wirklicher Name?« fragte K. »Gewiß«, war die Antwort, »warum haben Sie denn Zweifel?« »Ich dachte, Sie könnten Grund haben, Ihren Namen zu verschweigen«, sagte K. Er fühlte sich so frei, wie man es sonst nur ist, wenn man in der Fremde mit niedrigen Leuten spricht, alles, was einen selbst betrifft, bei sich behält, nur gleichmütig von den Interessen der anderen redet, sie dadurch vor sich selbst erhöht, aber auch nach Belieben fallen lassen kann. Bei der Tür des Arbeitszimmers des Advokaten blieb K. stehen, öffnete sie und rief dem Kaufmann, der folgsam weitergegangen war, zu: »Nicht so eilig! Leuchten Sie hier!« K. dachte, Leni könnte sich hier versteckt haben, er ließ den Kaufmann alle Winkel absuchen, aber das Zimmer war leer. Vor dem Bild des Richters hielt K. den Kaufmann hinten an den Hosenträgern zurück. »Kennen Sie den?« fragte er und zeigte mit dem Zeigefinger in die Höhe. Der Kaufmann hob die Kerze, sah blinzelnd hinauf und sagte: »Es ist ein Richter.« »Ein hoher Richter?« fragte K. und stellte sich seitlich vor den Kaufmann, um den Eindruck, den das Bild auf ihn machte, zu beobachten. Der Kaufmann sah bewundernd aufwärts. »Es ist ein hoher Richter«, sagte er. »Sie haben keinen großen Einblick«, sagte K. »Unter den niedrigen Untersuchungsrichtern ist er der niedrigste.« »Nun erinnere ich mich«, sagte der Kaufmann und senkte die Kerze, »ich habe es auch schon gehört.« »Aber natürlich«, rief K., »ich vergaß ja, natürlich müssen Sie es schon gehört haben.« »Aber warum denn, warum denn«? fragte der Kaufmann, während er sich, von K. mit den Händen angetrieben, zur Tür fortbewegte. Draußen auf dem Gang sagte K.: »Sie wissen doch, wo sich Leni versteckt hat?« »Versteckt?« sagte der Kaufmann, »nein, sie dürfte aber in der Küche sein und dem Advokaten eine Suppe kochen.« »Warum haben Sie das nicht gleich gesagt?« fragte K. »Ich wollte Sie ja hinführen, Sie haben mich aber wieder zurückgerufen«, antwortete der Kaufmann, wie verwirrt durch die widersprechenden Befehle. »Sie glauben wohl sehr schlau zu sein«, sagte K., »führen Sie mich also!« In der Küche war K. noch nie gewesen, sie war überraschend groß und reich ausgestattet. Allein der Herd war dreimal so groß wie gewöhnliche Herde, von dem übrigen sah man keine Einzelheiten, denn die Küche wurde jetzt nur von einer kleinen Lampe beleuchtet, die beim Eingang hing. Am Herd stand Leni in weißer Schürze, wie immer, und leerte Eier in einen Topf aus, der auf einem Spiritusfeuer stand. »Guten Abend, Josef«, sagte sie mit einem Seitenblick. »Guten Abend«, sagte K. und zeigte mit einer Hand auf einen abseits stehenden Sessel, auf den sich der Kaufmann setzen sollte, was dieser auch tat. K. aber ging ganz nahe hinter Leni, beugte sich über ihre Schulter und fragte: »Wer ist der Mann?« Leni umfaßte K. mit einer Hand, die andere quirlte die Suppe, zog ihn nach vorn zu sich und sagte: »Es ist ein bedauernswerter Mensch, ein armer Kaufmann, ein gewisser Block. Sieh ihn nur an.« Sie blickten beide zurück. Der Kaufmann saß auf dem Sessel, auf den ihn K. gewiesen hatte, er hatte die Kerze, deren Licht jetzt unnötig war, ausgepustet und drückte mit den Fingern den Docht, um den Rauch zu verhindern. »Du warst im Hemd«, sagte K. und wendete ihren Kopf mit der Hand wieder dem Herd zu. Sie schwieg. »Er ist dein Geliebter?« fragte K. Sie wollte nach dem Suppentopf greifen, aber K. nahm ihre beiden Hände und sagte: »Nun antworte!« Sie sagte: »Komm ins Arbeitszimmer, ich werde dir alles erklären.« »Nein«, sagte K., »ich will, daß du es hier erklärst.« Sie hing sich an ihn und wollte ihn küssen. K. wehrte sie aber ab und sagte: »Ich will nicht, daß du mich jetzt küßt.« »Josef«, sagte Leni und sah K. bittend und doch offen in die Augen, »du wirst doch nicht auf Herrn Block eifersüchtig sein. – Rudi«, sagte sie dann, sich an den Kaufmann wendend, »so hilf mir doch, du siehst, ich werde verdächtigt, laß die Kerze.« Man hätte denken können, er hätte nicht achtgegeben, aber er war vollständig eingeweiht. »Ich wüßte auch nicht, warum Sie eifersüchtig sein sollten«, sagte er wenig schlagfertig. »Ich weiß es eigentlich auch nicht«, sagte K. und sah den Kaufmann lächelnd an. Leni lachte laut, benützte die Unaufmerksamkeit K.s, um sich in seinen Arm einzuhängen, und flüsterte: »Laß ihn jetzt, du siehst ja, was für ein Mensch er ist. Ich habe mich seiner ein wenig angenommen, weil er eine große Kundschaft des Advokaten ist, aus keinem andern Grund. Und du? Willst du noch heute mit dem Advokaten sprechen? Er ist heute sehr krank, aber wenn du willst, melde ich dich doch an. Über Nacht bleibst du aber bei mir, ganz gewiß. Du warst auch schon so lange nicht bei uns, selbst der Advokat hat nach dir gefragt. Vernachlässige den Prozeß nicht! Auch ich habe dir Verschiedenes mitzuteilen, was ich erfahren habe. Nun aber zieh fürs erste deinen Mantel aus!« Sie half ihm, sich ausziehen, nahm ihm den Hut ab, lief mit den Sachen ins Vorzimmer, sie anzuhängen, lief dann wieder zurück und sah nach der Suppe. »Soll ich zuerst dich anmelden oder ihm zuerst die Suppe bringen?« »Melde mich zuerst an«, sagte K. Er war ärgerlich, er hatte ursprünglich beabsichtigt, mit Leni seine Angelegenheit, insbesondere die fragliche Kündigung genau zu besprechen, die Anwesenheit des Kaufmanns hatte ihm aber die Lust dazu genommen. Jetzt aber hielt er seine Sache doch für zu wichtig, als daß dieser kleine Kaufmann vielleicht entscheidend eingreifen sollte, und so rief er Leni, die schon auf dem Gang war, wieder zurück. »Bring ihm doch zuerst die Suppe«, sagte er, »er soll sich für die Unterredung mit mir stärken, er wird es nötig haben.« »Sie sind auch ein Klient des Advokaten«, sagte, wie zur Feststellung, der Kaufmann leise aus seiner Ecke. Es wurde aber nicht gut aufgenommen. »Was kümmert Sie denn das?« sagte K., und Leni sagte: »Wirst du still sein. – Dann bringe ich ihm also zuerst die Suppe«, sagte Leni zu K. und goß die Suppe auf einen Teller. »Es ist dann nur zu befürchten, daß er bald einschläft, nach dem Essen schläft er bald ein.« »Das, was ich ihm sagen werde, wird ihn wacherhalten«, sagte K., er wollte immerfort durchblicken lassen, daß er etwas Wichtiges mit dem Advokaten zu verhandeln beabsichtige, er wollte von Leni gefragt werden, was es sei, und dann erst sie um Rat fragen. Aber sie erfüllte pünktlich bloß die ausgesprochenen Befehle. Als sie mit der Tasse an ihm vorüberging, stieß sie absichtlich sanft an ihn und flüsterte: »Wenn er die Suppe gegessen hat, melde ich dich gleich an, damit ich dich möglichst bald wiederbekomme.« »Geh nur«, sagte K., »geh nur.« »Sei doch freundlicher«, sagte sie und drehte sich in der Tür mit der Tasse nochmals ganz um.
